Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
23:06:40 UTC
08:06:40 KST

Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
This post (and the code behind it) was written with a lot of help from AI. I'm not going to apologize for that. If that bothers you, feel free to close the tab.
I maintain Ratatui, so I see a lot of the TUIs people build. Many of them end up looking fairly same-ish: plain boxes on a boring background, missing a bunch of the things that good design in other mediums brings us.
Borders are part of the problem. They have to take up space, so they become part of the panels
people want to build. One option is to drop them and just use color, but borders are really nice
for delineating and surrounding things. There are lots of ways to sort of get borders in a
terminal, but none that are 100% good. I've drawn enough ┌──┐ by hand to have opinions about
this.
The usual way is the Unicode Box Drawing block, which has 128 characters for lines, corners and joins. Somehow that's still not enough:
So I've been working on a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells instead. I've got it working as a patch to Ghostty (and an earlier version in Rio before that), and I've built demo apps for it with Ratatui. I'd like feedback from terminal and TUI authors.
Every line in that screenshot is a cell border. None of them use up a row or column. The tab labels sit on the top edge of each pane, the text fields are underlined right under the text, and the buttons are one row tall and rounded.
Here's the same app in a terminal without cell borders, falling back to box-drawing characters:
Each pane loses a row and a column on every side, so the log pane shows two fewer lines and the notes wrap differently. The tab labels move inside the frame. The text fields use the underline attribute instead, and the checkbox and buttons turn into brackets.
What I'd use it for
- Borders, obviously. Panes and panels that don't eat a row and column on every side.
- Menus and popups that sit on top of other content and still look like they're on top.
- Panel style apps, where the layout is a set of regions that each want an edge.
- Widgets like text fields, buttons and checkboxes, which want a line right up against their text.
- Making things look neater in general. A border on the outer edge of a panel's background looks a lot cleaner, and text can run right up to it.
Up close
The settings form, with cell borders and then with the box-drawing fallback:
The tabs are the same story. With cell borders they sit on the pane's top edge. With box characters they need their own row inside the frame:
Charts
Lines between cells also work for charts. btop-style braille graphs fill every cell with dots, so there's nowhere to put a gridline or an average line without giving up a row. With cell borders they sit on the cell edges between the dots. Here's a monitor in that style, built with Ratatui:
And the fallback, which has to drop the gridlines:
In motion
Here's the tiling panes demo moving panes around, opening menus and the about dialog:
Partway through, it turns on a checkerboard of the cells, which shows how everything lines up with the grid. Toggle it here:
What box characters can't do
The root of it is that box-drawing characters are text. Each line is a glyph that takes up a whole cell, and pretty much everything annoying about them falls out of that.
Space is the obvious one. On my 16" laptop with a font I can actually read, the terminal is something like 200x50 (your prefs will move that around a bit). Columns are mostly fine at that size. Rows aren't. A layout with a couple of levels of nested panels can easily spend 6 or 8 of those 50 rows on nothing but lines. That's a lot of screen to give up for decoration.
You also can't put a line between two cells that both have something in them. So there's no way to underline a text field right under its text, or to outline a button, without adding padding around it. Rounded corners sort of work, except the corner glyph has one background color, and when the panel's background is different from what's around it you get a little square of the wrong color in each corner. And the line itself is whatever the font decides it is, weight and position included.
Then there's copy and paste. Select some text inside a box and you get the box too. Everyone who's
pasted from a TUI into Slack knows the little │ cleanup dance. Sometimes you do want the box
(pasting a table into a chat, say), but mostly it's junk. Cell borders aren't text, so they never
get copied, which cuts both ways.
How it works
A cell border is a cell attribute, like a background color. Each cell can carry up to twelve line segments: the two halves of each of its four edges, and four arms from its center. Each segment has its own color, width, placement and style, and the terminal draws them over the cell grid. Borders are stored in the cells, so they scroll, erase, insert and reflow with the text. What happens on erase or scroll already has an answer, the same one as for colors.
The edges are split into halves so borders line up with quadrant block characters (▖▗▘▝ and
friends). That makes it easy to draw a shape that's a half cell in from the grid and still put a
neat border around it. Yes, that still uses a character for the fill, and there might be a better
way to do that part. One problem at a time.
The same idea could stretch to sextants and octants, or to quarter and eighth widths, if designs need them.
Styles and joints
Lines can be solid, double, dashed or dotted. Each corner and center of a cell can be square or rounded, with a configurable radius and anti-aliased arcs. A rounded corner can name an outside color, so the area outside the arc is painted correctly when the panel's background differs from what's behind it.
When two neighboring cells both put a line on their shared edge, they merge into one line. The
stroke with the higher priority wins, then the wider one, then the one to the right or below.
That way a focused pane can raise its priority and keep its whole outline, whatever order its
neighbors were drawn in. My first try was "right/bottom always wins", which lasted until the
focused pane lost half its outline to its neighbor.
The wire format
Everything is one DCS string with a namespace:
ESC P 1 + b cell-border ; OP ; FIELDS... ESC \
The common path is a pen, held in the cursor like the current background color. Set it, print some text, and the printed cells get the borders:
ESC P 1 + b cell-border;pen;48;32;7aa2f7;0;0 ESC \     bottom edge, blue: an underline
hello
ESC [ 0 m                                              SGR 0 clears the pen
There are also rectangle commands that set or clear borders on existing cells without touching
the pen, and a capability query. An app sends the query followed by DA1. If the DA1 reply arrives
without a cell-border reply first, the terminal doesn't support it, so the app falls back to box
characters and reserves the space they need. Terminals that don't understand the DCS ignore it,
the same as any unknown DCS.
The minimum a terminal needs is the pen, the rectangle commands and solid strokes. I've tried to keep that first cut small, because there's always one more "... and this" to add, and that's a slippery slope.
Line styles, rounded joints, priority and outside colors are extension fields listed in the capability reply, and unknown fields are ignored, so they can be added later. I'd rather the early decisions be two way doors where possible.
The spec calls itself version 1 (it's the 1 in DCS 1 + b). That's v1 in the old sense, before
we all got bogged down in semver. It doesn't mean done or stable, it means it's the first one I was willing to write
down. Read it as v0.1, or a draft, or whatever you prefer.
Prior art
Parts of this have been done before:
- DEC ruled lines in DECterm (extension 43 in the DA1 reply) draw lines around rectangles. They scroll with the text, but they're a separate layer: clearing the screen leaves them behind, and they're always one pixel wide in the normal text color.
- SGR 51 to 65: framed, encircled, overline and the ideogram side lines. Some terminals draw borders with them, but they're on/off attributes with no color, width or joins, and there's no attribute for the bottom edge.
- The Win32 console has per-cell grid flags for the top, left and right edges. PDCurses
and X/Open curses (WA_TOP, WA_LEFT and friends) have similar attributes. These are the
closest to this protocol, but they have no bottom edge (Win32), color, width or halves.
- IBM 3270 terminals can outline whole input fields.
What none of these give you is a line with its own color and width on each edge. The rationale document covers the prior art in more detail and explains each choice in the protocol.
My own first prototype was in Rio (raphamorim/rio#1947), with an earlier version of the spec that used APC instead of DCS. Feedback pointed out that APC isn't safe to reuse: Kermit 95 has run APC payloads as Kermit commands since the 90s. DCS is where structured terminal commands already live, and terminals ignore DCS strings they don't recognize, so I switched to that.
The awkward (edge) cases
When I first showed this around, most of the questions were about these. The spec goes into all of them properly, but here's roughly where I landed.
Multiplexers were the first thing people asked about. tmux and friends redraw panes from their own idea of the cell grid, so passing these sequences through would just put borders in the wrong place. A multiplexer that doesn't know about the protocol should drop them and answer DA1 itself, and then apps running inside it fall back to box characters like they would anywhere else. One that does know about it can store borders like any other attribute and redraw them.
Conflicting lines on a shared edge are settled when the terminal renders, using the priority rule above, so it doesn't matter what order the app wrote the cells in.
Erase, insert and delete all work the way they do for background colors. Erased cells pick up the current pen, and lines that get inserted or deleted take their borders along. Scrollback, the alternate screen and reflow mostly come for free, because the border lives in the cell.
On cost: the Ghostty change is about 1,650 lines, and a fair chunk of that is tests. Each cell gets a 16-bit border ID, which fits in padding that was already there, so cells don't get any bigger and a screen with no borders costs nothing extra. The IDs point into a table of distinct border sets (about 100 bytes each) that's shared by the whole terminal. A typical TUI only uses a handful of distinct sets, but the table is never freed, so in the worst case (all 65,535 IDs in use) it's somewhere around 10-15 MB.
Rendering only does extra work for cells that have borders. Each one looks at its four neighbors to resolve shared edges, so changing a row also rebuilds the rows either side of it. Straight lines are a few solid quads per cell. Rounded corners cost more, because the anti-aliased arc is drawn as rows of small quads, roughly one per edge pixel. I haven't benchmarked any of this properly yet, and it's the part I'd most like another set of eyes on.
Try it
The spec and rationale are on my Ghostty fork. The Ghostty branch implements all of version 1. I've only built and run it on macOS so far, so the GTK and OpenGL builds are untested. To build and run it (you'll need Zig 0.17 and Xcode):
git clone -b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ghostty.git
cd ghostty
zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dxcframework-target=native
open zig-out/Ghostty.app
Inside that Ghostty, the gallery script on the same branch draws the style gallery above. It detects support first, so it's also a quick check for another terminal's implementation:
python3 scripts/cell-borders.py            # the default view
python3 scripts/cell-borders.py --styles   # line styles, joints and outside fill
Once it's running you can flip between views with keys: p placement, c colors, h blocks, j
junctions, e halves, s styles and l live. w cycles the stroke width, b turns borders off
so you can compare, and q quits. Each view also has a matching flag (--placement, --styles
and so on) if you want to start on it.
The tiling panes demo is on the Ratatui branch. It falls back to box-drawing characters when the terminal doesn't support cell borders, which is how I made the comparison shots above:
git clone -b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ratatui.git
cd ratatui
cargo run -p tiling-panes
Drag panes around with the mouse to retile them. n and v split, x closes, and right click
opens a pane menu. Press b to switch between cell borders and box drawing, or g to shade
alternate cells and see where the edges are.
The btop-style monitor from the chart screenshots is in the same branch. Given how much of it an AI wrote, I did briefly consider calling it bslop:
To run it:
cargo run -p cell-border-top
It's a real system monitor (it reads your actual CPU, memory, network and processes), so it's a
better test of how this looks on a busy screen than the panes demo. 1 to 4 show and hide the
boxes, b and g work the same as in the panes demo, and h or ? lists the rest of the keys.
It needs a newer Rust (1.95) than the rest of Ratatui because of the sysinfo dependency.
What I'd like to hear
I'm not attached to this being the exact solution, but I think it's a problem worth solving, and I'd like it to be more than one terminal's feature (and more than one weekend's worth of yak shaving). If you work on a terminal, would you implement this, and which parts look expensive? If you work on a TUI library or app, which of your widgets would use it, and what would they need that isn't here? Comments are welcome on the Ghostty discussion.

Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
23:06:40 UTC
08:06:40 KST

Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
This post (and the code behind it) was written with a lot of help from AI. I'm not going to apologize for that. If that bothers you, feel free to close the tab.
I maintain Ratatui, so I see a lot of the TUIs people build. Many of them end up looking fairly same-ish: plain boxes on a boring background, missing a bunch of the things that good design in other mediums brings us.
Borders are part of the problem. They have to take up space, so they become part of the panels
people want to build. One option is to drop them and just use color, but borders are really nice
for delineating and surrounding things. There are lots of ways to sort of get borders in a
terminal, but none that are 100% good. I've drawn enough ┌──┐ by hand to have opinions about
this.
The usual way is the Unicode Box Drawing block, which has 128 characters for lines, corners and joins. Somehow that's still not enough:
So I've been working on a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells instead. I've got it working as a patch to Ghostty (and an earlier version in Rio before that), and I've built demo apps for it with Ratatui. I'd like feedback from terminal and TUI authors.
Every line in that screenshot is a cell border. None of them use up a row or column. The tab labels sit on the top edge of each pane, the text fields are underlined right under the text, and the buttons are one row tall and rounded.
Here's the same app in a terminal without cell borders, falling back to box-drawing characters:
Each pane loses a row and a column on every side, so the log pane shows two fewer lines and the notes wrap differently. The tab labels move inside the frame. The text fields use the underline attribute instead, and the checkbox and buttons turn into brackets.

- Borders, obviously. Panes and panels that don't eat a row and column on every side.

How Not to Build a Music Player
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
23:04:30 UTC
08:04:30 KST

The Twelve-Day War made me realize online music players aren’t a viable option for those who live under an oppressive regime that disconnects the internet across the country as a way to silence public opinion.
So, as soon as the connection came back, I started archiving tracks and looking for offline alternatives and discovered Strawberry. It’s a feature-rich music player and kept me happy for quite a while, but I have this habit of looking at song lyrics and singing along! Strawberry fetches lyrics from the internet when it recognizes a song, but sometimes the lyrics weren’t line-synced and worse, it displayed the timestamps next to the lyrics which I found pretty annoying to look at. I wasn’t aware of other music players such as foobar2000 which my friend just pointed me to while writing this post.
I decided to write my own music player and call it AMP with a few goals in mind: minimal feature-set, no C++ dependencies, proper system integration to make it feel like a native app, and of course, write it in Zig (including the shaders!). I also wanted to roll my own UI because of the fun memories of working on V’s UI during my first days of being introduced into system programming. But before I could make any meaningful progress, a new wave of protests started. Following the tragedy of January 8 and 9, another internet blackout began, lasting more than four months.
During the blackout, there were these anonymous people on Telegram selling internet access through personal White SIMs, whitelisted servers, Starlink dishes, etc. A black market had formed for the freaking internet! You’d get charged $5 or more for just 1GB of traffic. The prices dropped slightly after a while, but it was still hella expensive. The regime surely made a lot of money out of it. I ended up spending hundreds of dollars on these services and other methods just to stay in touch with my friends and keep my hobbies alive. Killing time was becoming a problem. Especially for someone like me who built their entire social life online.
I carefully used this slow connection to download repositories, documention, etc. to continue working on my music player. It really brought me immense joy during this hard time.
Once the connection was mostly restored to the pre-blackout days (UDP traffic is still blocked, though, which naturally also affects QUIC), my attention was shifted towards LLMs. It had become very hard for me to ignore the hype and progress around frontier LLMs. As I really never thought about using them seriously for coding. They are still everywhere in the news, and I was just reminded that I owned a Claude Max 20x subscription gift from my boss back in 2025. Eating dust and maybe soon expiring. So I decided to give it a try and experiment on my music player. It was a very addictive experience. I literally couldn’t hit the plan limits no matter how hard I tried, so after a few non-stop days of prompting, a good chunk of AMP was vibecoded..
At the time, I thought this was an okay approach for a hobby project and I could just un-slopify it later. Little did I know I’m mentally incapable of reviewing tens of thousands lines of code. Shortly after, Anthropic figured that I live in Iran and instantly banned my account. Then Codeberg announced its no-AI policy, which gave me two choices. Either get rid of all that slop or move the repository elsewhere. Going with the former option, I started reading every single line of code, rewriting them. I was surprised by my own ignorance and how much LLMs like to complicate stuff. (I wish I could show an example, but my memory is extremely fragile and I’ve got no pre-rewrite history of the repo to check).
Four months later, nearly half the codebase is gone, and somehow it’s more robust with the same set of features (and more). I regret relying on LLMs in the first place, but hey, lesson learned. That said I think it’s still possible to create a healthy relationship with LLMs as long as you look at them as a fancy IDE feature. A lot of times they are just running long sed or regex commands that are a no-brainer act for humans when done by hand but still consumes a good time. For now and hopefully forever I think I’ll be going the old school way. Never rush your hobbies!
Btw this is how AMP looks like right now!
Worth mentioning that the blur shader is written in Zig based on this excellent blog post!.
Roadmap to v1.0:
- Music server
- Android and Windows support
- Packaging for major Linux distros
- Any suggestions?

I ended up spending hundreds of dollars on these services and other methods just to stay in touch with my friends and keep my hobbies alive. Killing time was becoming a problem. Especially for someone like me who built their entire social life online.
I carefully used this slow connection to download repositories, documention, etc. to continue working on my music player. It really brought me immense joy during this hard time.
Once the connection was mostly restored to the pre-blackout days (UDP traffic is still blocked, though, which naturally also affects QUIC), my attention was shifted towards LLMs. It had become very hard for me to ignore the hype and progress around frontier LLMs. As I really never thought about using them seriously for coding. They are still everywhere in the news, and I was just reminded that I owned a Claude Max 20x subscription gift from my boss back in 2025. Eating dust and maybe soon expiring. So I decided to give it a try and experiment on my music player. It was a very addictive experience. I literally couldn’t hit the plan limits no matter how hard I tried, so after a few non-stop days of prompting, a good chunk of AMP was vibecoded..
At the time, I thought this was an okay approach for a hobby project and I could just un-slopify it later. Little did I know I’m mentally incapable of reviewing tens of thousands lines of code. Shortly after, Anthropic figured that I live in Iran and instantly banned my account. Then Codeberg announced its no-AI policy, which gave me two choices. Either get rid of all that slop or move the repository elsewhere. Going with the former option, I started reading every single line of code, rewriting them. I was surprised by my own ignorance and how much LLMs like to complicate stuff. (I wish I could show an example, but my memory is extremely fragile and I’ve got no pre-rewrite history of the repo to check).
Four months later, nearly half the codebase is gone, and somehow it’s more robust with the same set of features (and more). I regret relying on LLMs in the first place, but hey, lesson learned. That said I think it’s still possible to create a healthy relationship with LLMs as long as you look at them as a fancy IDE feature. A lot of times they are just running long sed or regex commands that are a no-brainer act for humans when done by hand but still consumes a good time. For now and hopefully forever I think I’ll be going the old school way. Never rush your hobbies!
Btw this is how AMP looks like right now!
Worth mentioning that the blur shader is written in Zig based on this excellent blog post!.
Roadmap to v1.0:
- Music server
- Android and Windows support
- Packaging for major Linux distros
- Any suggestions?

Lego's BrickLink Marketplace Back Online After Week-Long Outage Caused By 'Cyber Incident' (brickfanatics.com) 3
			
		 	
				LEGO's BrickLink marketplace is back online after a week-long outage caused by what the company described as a "cyber incident," during which an unauthorized third party accessed some user data. Details about exactly what data was accessed remain unclear. The site went offline on November 5 and remained unavailable until November 12, preventing users from buying or selling LEGO sets and parts during the busy holiday shopping season. According to Brick Fanatics, LEGO initially described the outage as "necessary work" before confirming that the platform had suffered a security incident.
In an email to users, LEGO acknowledged that "some of the information associated with your account was accessed and disclosed by an unauthorized party," including potentially usernames and IP addresses. However, the company insisted that "your password, postal address, and financial information were not disclosed." Those assurances have since come under scrutiny following reports of convincing phishing emails containing detailed personal and purchase information.
The outage also dealt a significant blow to independent sellers who rely on BrickLink for income. Simon Webster, who operates stores on both BrickLink and rival marketplace Brick Owl, reported that his overall sales revenue fell 52% over a four-day period, even as sales through Brick Owl rose 79%. "Their comms are amateur at the best of times, but surely they should be able to send an email to let sellers and buyers alike know what is happening and what they're doing to rectify it," Webster said. "But no, we're all left in the dark."
The incident has renewed concerns about BrickLink's aging infrastructure. Founded in 2000 and acquired by LEGO in 2019, the marketplace reportedly runs on a complex collection of interconnected systems that makes modernization difficult. The Brick Fanatics report questions whether the 25-year-old platform remains fit for purpose and whether prolonged outages and security concerns could push sellers toward competing marketplaces like Brick Owl.

Lying to Zed to get its remote server running on FreeBSD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
22:54:47 UTC
07:54:47 KST

I’ve used VS Code since I was about 16, so for almost ten years and honestly it was mostly fine. But as of late it has become unbearable: slow, and increasingly weighed down by AI slop. grahamperrin@ pointed out to me that VS Code now has chat.disableAIFeatures, and they’re right. I totally missed it! It really does turn the built-in AI features off atleast from what I can see in limited testing, and it works. But even with it off, VS Code still feels clunky as hell. Zed, on the other hand, is fast, and it had a native switch that turns all of its AI stuff off slightly earlier than VS Code did, which I absolutely adore. (It’s a toggle in Settings, or "disable_ai": true in your settings file.)
That’s not because I avoid LLMs. I just don’t want them trying to edit every line I write, or sitting in the corner judging me ominously. I still write most of my FOSS code myself: it keeps me sane, and I feel FOSS developers have a responsibility to keep code clean for LLMs to steal from lol. What I do hand off is the tiring part: regression testing, edge cases, and exploration beyond what my tiny 20-watt brain can hold. For that I use harnesses that work well with models, like OpenCode. Beyond auto-complete.. I’ve always found entire harnesses like claude code etc. very clunky in editors.
Getting it working
Zed has no FreeBSD remote server offering (yet), but FreeBSD can run Linux binaries in spades, so we use Zed’s Linux one. All you need is a FreeBSD server you can SSH into.
1. Turn on Linux compatibility
sudo sysrc linux_enable=YES
sudo service linux start
sudo pkg install linux_base-rl9
kldstat -m linux64    # should print a module
2. Make Zed pick the Linux server
Zed asks the host what platform it runs. FreeBSD says FreeBSD amd64, there’s no server for that, and Zed gives up. This wrapper says Linux x86_64 to that one question and passes everything else to the real uname. Save it as ~/.local/bin/uname and make it executable:
#!/bin/sh
case "$#:$*" in
  1:-sm|1:-ms) printf 'Linux x86_64\n' ;;
  *) exec /usr/bin/uname "$@" ;;
esac
Put ~/.local/bin on PATH for non-interactive SSH sessions. For zsh, add this to ~/.zshenv (use your shell’s equivalent):
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
It’s a small lie, but a contained one, and the part I’d love to retire.
3. Connect.
Connect over SSH from Zed and open a folder. The first connection uploads the Linux server to ~/.zed_server/. To watch, run tail -f ~/.local/share/zed/logs/server-workspace-*.log.
4. Run a kernel with the (FreeBSD) fix
Without it you’ll connect fine and get an empty project tree, with this in the server log:
error processing entry failed to read directory entry
Caused by:
    Invalid argument (os error 22)
The fix is ec6629628cb, in main, stable/15 and releng/15.2, so 15.2-RELEASE will include it. If the error persists, check you booted the new kernel with uname -v.
The bug in layman terms
To show your project, Zed asks the server for the names of the files in each folder, a few at a time. Zed sets aside a small amount of space for each batch.
Picture a teacher reading a class roll to a student who writes the names on a sticky note (I couldn’t come up with a better analogy, bare with me). The teacher crosses off each name as she reads it, and she never reads a crossed-off name again. The student’s note has room for 6 names. The teacher reads in groups of 4, a sensible habit that works fine almost every time. But 6 isn’t a whole number of groups, so she reads 8 names and crosses all 8 off. Only 6 fit on the note.
Now she’s in a bind. Her slip was grabbing more than fit before checking. She can’t hand over the 6 that fit and keep the other 2 for later, because they’re already crossed off and she would never read them again. So she reports an error instead, which at least is loud. When I tried the quiet way, 112 of my 1,002 files vanished (from the listing) with no warning. A loud error beats a quiet loss I’m pretty sure. Zed saw the error and decided it couldn’t read the folder, and showed it up empty.
The fix is small: read no more names than fit on the note. Read 6, cross off 6, come back for the next 6, until the roll is done. In the real bug, the teacher is FreeBSD’s Linux translator (Linuxulator), the note is a 768-byte buffer, and a group of 4 names is a 512-byte block.
For the kernel nerds
This is a regression. A February 2026 fix for NFS directories returning bogus entries (110f2567cb51, PR 292282) changed how sys/compat/linux/linux_file.c sizes its native read, in both linux_getdents() and linux_getdents64():
/* before February 2026 */
buflen = min(args->count, MAXBSIZE);
/* after: every request rounded up to a 512-byte block */
buflen = min(roundup2(args->count, DEV_BSIZE), MAXBSIZE);
If the caller’s buffer isn’t a multiple of 512 bytes, the native batch can outgrow it. The emulation layer converts records until one doesn’t fit and returns EINVAL, but kern_getdirentries() has already advanced the directory offset past the whole batch. That’s why returning a partial batch isn’t enough on its own.
The fix (ec6629628cb, reviewed in D60760):
if (args->count >= DEV_BSIZE)
	buflen = min(args->count, MAXBSIZE);
else
	buflen = roundup2(args->count, DEV_BSIZE);
It’s safe because Linux directory records are never larger than FreeBSD’s: for dirent64 the header is 19 bytes against 24, and both round each record up to a multiple of 8. A native batch that fits in the caller’s buffer translates into one that fits too.
Legacy getdents had the same bug for 32-bit and 64-bit callers. My first patch only fixed getdents64; fixing both took the test matrix from 86 failures to zero.
Acknowledgements
I’ve had plenty of patches merged before this one, but this was among the quickest to land in releng/15.2: it didn’t sit in stable for long (thankfully!). The release engineering team (re@) runs a really cool process that I am yet to fully understand in depth. Thank you also to Kyle Evans (kevans@) and Mark Johnston (markj@) for reviewing the patch and for their notes along the way.

Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
22:43:00 UTC
07:43:00 KST

It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.
Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.
Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.
“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.
Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.
Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.
“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”
Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.
For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.
“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”
It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.
If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)
Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.
Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.
While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.
Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.
Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.
“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.
Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

Claude Meetings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
22:39:15 UTC
07:39:15 KST

Introducing Claude Meetings
Add Claude to your video call and get the work started while you talk
Claude can now join your video calls as a visible participant, follow the conversation and start on work during the meeting. Claude Meetings is now in beta.
Your team can ask Claude questions during the meeting, out loud or in chat. By default, Claude answers in writing, and it can use your connected tools with your permission.
Claude also works with you live to build docs, whiteboards (opens in new tab), or other artifacts, while teammates on the invite refine them. Claude writes the notes and action items, so no one on the call has to.
Claude Meetings is starting to roll out in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Support for other video conferencing platforms is coming soon.
What it looks like
Say your team is planning a customer event, and Claude is on the call. You say, “Claude, start a doc for this plan.” Claude writes up what the team has said so far, and teammates on the invite can edit the plan while you keep talking.
When you start discussing the budget, someone asks Claude what last year’s event cost. Claude asks for their approval to look it up, posts it in the meeting chat, and compares it to the current plan. When you start discussing timelines, someone asks Claude to put it on a whiteboard, and the team works on the schedule alongside the doc.
Before the meeting ends, someone asks Claude to share a recap with the team. After the call, any notes, action items, plan, and whiteboard are on the meeting’s page in claude.ai (opens in new tab).
Later, you can go back to meetings you were part of and ask Claude about them, or add Claude to the next one from your calendar in claude.ai.
We’re working with partners like Gong, Attention, Granola, Fireflies.ai, Otter, and Plaud, so you’ll soon be able to send a meeting’s transcript to the tools your team already uses.
Security and privacy
Claude adds a separate page for each meeting in claude.ai (opens in new tab) with the notes, transcript, and anything it built. People from your organization on the invite can see it and edit what Claude made, and it can be shared with others in your organization from the page.
By default, Claude is set to stay out of calls when someone from outside your organization is invited, and to leave if someone from outside joins partway through. An admin can allow Claude on calls with outside guests. On those calls, Claude posts its notice in the call’s chat but doesn’t reply there, and what guests say is included in the notes and transcript.
Claude uses each person’s connected tools with that person’s permission. It asks the first time, and a yes applies going forward. For now, when someone asks out loud, Claude asks each time to confirm who’s speaking. An answer posted in the call’s chat is visible to everyone on the call.
When Claude joins, it appears as a participant and posts a notice in the call’s chat. It saves a transcript, summary, and screen descriptions, not audio.
Before you add Claude or turn on auto-join, make sure everyone on your calls is OK with being transcribed.
Getting started
Claude joins when someone adds it or has auto-join on. Support is currently available for Google Meet, with other platforms coming soon. On Team plans, inviting Claude to your meetings is available by default, and an admin can turn it off. On Enterprise plans, an admin turns it on for all or part of the organization. While it’s in beta, it isn’t available to some organizations, including those with zero data retention (ZDR), HIPAA-ready configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).
During the beta, Claude’s notes and transcripts are free on Team and Enterprise plans. So are its answers in your calls, unless an answer uses one of your connected tools, which counts toward your plan’s usage. The docs, whiteboards, (opens in new tab) and other artifacts Claude makes in a call are free through February 10, 2027.
Setup steps are in the Help Center.

Home Assistant: the password is not the key – token secrets in cleartext
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
22:30:10 UTC
07:30:10 KST

Full Disclosure mailing list archives
Home Assistant: the password is not the key — token secrets in cleartext, two token classes never expire, password change revokes none (2026.11.0, live-proven)
From: theknell--- via Fulldisclosure <fulldisclosure () seclists org>
Date: Sun, 08 Nov 2026 11:02:24 -0500
Home Assistant's documentation tells users: "Your password is the key
to your home, so choose a strong, unique one." Home Assistant is
installed in two million homes by the vendor's own published count,
and in those homes it holds the locks, the alarm, the garage, the
cameras, and the record of who is home.
The password is not the key. Tested against home-assistant/core
2026.11.0 (frontend 20261028.4, hass-nabucasa 2.8.1):
1. Every refresh token's secret and its per-token JWT signing key,
for every user, is serialized in cleartext in one file:
config/.storage/auth. Passwords in the neighbouring store are
bcrypt-hashed; token secrets are not hashed at all — validation
is a direct string comparison against the stored value.
2. Two of the three token classes never expire. Long-lived and
system refresh tokens are created with expire_at = None; the
long-lived access tokens the documentation recommends for scripts
are valid for ten years, and the core API accepts a caller-supplied
lifespan in days with no upper bound.
3. Changing the password revokes none of them. All four
password-change entry points — self-service, administrator,
Supervisor reset, command line — rehash the password record and
make no token call.
4. The automatic-backup password is persisted in plaintext in
.storage/backup, in the same directory every backup archives —
and every settings backup carries .storage/auth inside it, so a
restore resurrects backup-era tokens.
Live proof, against our own instance only: after a real, verified
password change, a refresh token copied from .storage/auth beforehand
still minted fresh access, and a ten-year long-lived token minted
beforehand still authenticated.
Scope, stated plainly: this is not an unauthenticated network break.
It begins with a read of the config directory or a backup. What it
shows is that any such read — a backup file shared for support, a
config folder synced somewhere it should not be, one file disclosure
anywhere in the stack — becomes durable, password-change-resistant
access to the home, and the one remediation every user reaches for
first, changing the password, does nothing.
Eleven documented claims were checked: 3 hold, 5 hold with a bound,
3 fall. What is sound is credited in the paper at the same weight:
the token generation entropy is impeccable, and access tokens live
thirty minutes.
Paper: https://archive.org/details/knell-not-the-key
Mirror: https://github.com/the-knell/not-the-key
Key: 133883AB9F6EDE5B9BA6B82E27BEDAF0CE152F25 (knell)
Verify: gpg --import knell-public.asc, then
gpg --verify paper-ha-FINAL-2026-11-04.md.asc
— knell
More, signed and timestamped: https://github.com/the-knell

“Store-Bought Pie Crust Is Actually Better”: Ina Garten Swears This Frozen One Tastes Homemade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13

“Store-Bought Pie Crust Is Actually Better”: Ina Garten Swears This Frozen One Tastes Homemade
Thanksgiving is next week (!), which means you’re likely planning your grocery store trip to grab all the ingredients for your big feast. One thing that absolutely has to be on the Thanksgiving menu is pie. (I’m partial to sweet potato pie, but pumpkin pie and pecan pie are always welcome.)
Ina Garten, queen of home cooking and entertaining, recently shared that she’ll be making her Bourbon Chocolate Pecan Pie this Thanksgiving, but what she said about the crust shocked us. In an Instagram post, she revealed that for once, store-bought isn’t just fine — it’s actually better!
“Making an old-fashioned Thanksgiving pie takes time, but this one is so much easier! I discovered that my Bourbon Chocolate Pecan Pie is actually better with a store-bought pie crust because it balances the richness of the filling (chocolate, pecans, and bourbon — what’s not to love?),” Ina wrote. “No mixer, just combine the ingredients in two bowls, pour them into the crust, and into the oven. The easiest Thanksgiving dessert ever will also be the biggest hit!!” she added.
If it’s good enough for Ina, it’s good enough for us. She didn’t reveal which pie crust was her favorite in the post, so we DM’d her in the hopes that she’d be willing to spill the deets. Lucky for us, she responded!
So what’s her favorite brand? Wholly Wholesome. The organic 9-inch pie shells come in a pack of two and are made in the USA with no animal ingredients (so they’re suitable for vegans), hydrogenated fats or oils, artificial colors, flavors, preservatives, or additives. You can purchase the pie crusts in select retailers or online at places like Amazon for $6.79.
She also revealed more on why she loves the store-bought pie crust in this YouTube video. Ina states, “I have this philosophy: If you can buy something really good at the store, or a bakery, there’s really no point in making it yourself.” (Hence, where the “store-bought is fine” catch phrase came from.) She goes on to share that while developing the bourbon pecan pie recipe, she tested it with a homemade pie crust and a store-bought pie crust, and came to the conclusion that the store-bought pie crust one was better.
But just because the pie crusts are store-bought doesn’t mean everyone has to know your secret. Ina suggests crimping the edges of the pie with a fork to give it that homemade look. And if you’re making her bourbon pecan pie recipe, be sure to defrost the pie shells overnight in the fridge before making your pie. The Barefoot Contessa strikes again — and your Thanksgiving just got a little bit easier.

US Seizes $1.2 Billion In Crypto Stolen From Binance (cnbc.com) 15
			
		 	
				U.S. authorities have seized or restrained more than $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen during Binance's $6 billion October hack, which the FBI attributes to North Korean military-linked hackers known as "TraderTraitor." The DOJ also said it disrupted infrastructure behind the "FaceStealer" deepfake scam, blamed for stealing more than $400 million in cryptocurrency. CNBC reports:  Collective efforts between the U.S. government and private sector have resulted in more than $2.7 billion of that amount being frozen. [...] The DOJ said it was taking coordinated action against what it called the North Korean government's "schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency." That includes "the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance," it said. DOJ units, law enforcement partners and virtual asset service providers have been working to intercept the stolen assets. But efforts to track and freeze the assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder them through various cryptocurrency channels.
Authorities have also seized cloud-based infrastructure used in a massive identity impersonation scam known as "FaceStealer," which has seen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen over 18 months, the DOJ said. The scheme sees hackers set up fake video meetings using stolen accounts and recordings of people known to the target by using AI-generated deepfakes. The hackers then say a technical problem requires a fix, install malware on a computer and take over the victim's communications, steal their cryptocurrency and target their contacts -- sometimes months or more than a year after the initial compromise.

The 3 Best Roasting Pans (I Cooked 25 Pounds of Chicken to Find Them!)
A roasting pan is one of those items in a home kitchen that might not get daily use, but is nevertheless a key piece of equipment for many home cooks. I only use my roasting pan once a year, but I use it to make arguably the main dish of the most important meal I’ll make all year: the Thanksgiving turkey. With that said, having a solid roasting pan — one that is sturdy, heats evenly, and is easy and secure to hold — is a non-negotiable in my kitchen.
Whether you’re cooking a holiday turkey, a prime rib, or even roasting off a sheet pan meal, a good roasting pan is key. To find the best of the best, I put five roasting pans through their paces and found three great options that will make reliable additions to your cookware collection for years to come.
Our Top Picks
- The Best Overall: Cuisinart MultiClad Pro 16” Roasting Pan ($159.95)
This thoughtfully designed roaster hit all the marks: sturdy construction; even cooking; wide, comfortable handles; a flat bottom; and well-shaped rack.
- The Best on a Budget: Farberware 12”x16” Nonstick Roaster ($39.99)
This heavy-gauge steel model has a strong rack with well-placed handles and a smooth nonstick surface that’s easy to clean; in our tests, it browned chicken beautifully.
- The Best Nonstick: Caraway Roasting Pan  ($179, $215)
A heavy-duty pan with a slick nonstick ceramic interior; this is the perfect choice if you’re looking for a stylish pan that doubles as serveware.

The Best Overall: Cuisinart MultiClad Pro 16” Roasting Pan
Cuisinart’s MultiClad Pro roasting pan hit all of my criteria. It’s sturdy enough to hold a large, heavy roast; the large handles feel secure and comfortable to hold; and the flat bottom meant that making gravy in it was a breeze. The body of the pan is made from a core of aluminum surrounded by stainless steel. This is the same three-ply construction employed in good stainless steel skillets that enables steady, even heat transfer. Chicken roasted up golden and moist, and the vegetables roasted underneath were well-browned and cooked evenly.
The U-shaped rack boasts its own wide handles and is strong enough to support the weight of a large piece of meat on its own — allowing you to lift the meat out of the roaster in order to use the pan to make gravy on the stovetop. The rack has legs that elevated the food on the rack (in this case, a whole chicken) between 1 and 1 1/2 inches from the bottom of the pan. That’s a comfortable height that meant I didn’t have any trouble fitting vegetables underneath.
The pan itself is compatible with all stovetops, including induction. The riveted handles (once cooled from their time in the oven) stayed cool to the touch while on the stovetop, allowing me to steady the pan with my hand while making gravy — no oven mitt necessary.
FYI

- The handles feel secure, but they’re a bit narrower than some of the other pans I’ve tested.

How We Tested Roasting Pans
- The roasted chicken test. I roasted a whole (4- to 6-pound) chicken in each pan with 2 pounds of vegetables underneath the roasting rack. The chicken was roasted until cooked through, then removed (still on the rack) and vegetables transferred out of the pan. I looked for how well the chicken was browned, whether it was moist, and took note of how long it took to cook all the way through. I noted how well the vegetables were cooked, whether they were browned evenly, and if they fit easily under the rack.
- The gravy test. Once the pan was empty, I placed each roasting pan over 2 burners of my gas stove and made gravy in the pan. I first made a roux with a mixture of the drippings in the pan, butter, and flour, and then added broth and whisked to make a smooth chicken gravy. I noted how easy or difficult it was to make gravy in the pan, whether the pan heated evenly on the stovetop, if it suffered any damage from being exposed to the direct heat of the stove, and whether ingredients got caught in any spots inside the pan.
- The cleaning test. I washed each pan by hand after testing to determine how easy they were to clean.
Why You Should Trust Me as a Tester
I am a seasoned food editor who has been working in professional kitchens for almost 15 years. I have been cooking Thanksgiving dinner, including roasting turkeys of varying sizes in roasting pans, for over a decade. In addition to my work as a chef, I’m a writer who has been testing and reviewing kitchen products for years.
What Makes the Best Roasting Pan
- Even cooking. Despite the fact that the main thing being cooked in a roasting pan is typically not in contact with the roasting pan itself, even distribution of heat is still key to success. The material the pan is made of, its depth, and the height of the sides of the pan all affect how the food will cook.
- Wide, secure handles. Roasting pans are often loaded down with large, heavy food, like a turkey, a prime rib, or a ham. It’s important to be able to hold the pan securely and transfer it in and out of the oven, with oven mitts or kitchen towels protecting your hands.
- A well-designed rack. For most people a roasting pan is something that is mainly used for big, heavy roasts (think: Thanksgiving turkeys, Christmas lamb racks or prime rib roasts, and Easter hams). It’s crucially important, in my opinion, to be able to lift that large piece of meat out of the pan easily so that you can access the vegetables underneath and/or make gravy on the stovetop. A flat rack just doesn’t allow you to do that. Angled racks also hold food in place better than flat ones, which makes transferring the pan between oven, stovetop, and table feel more secure.
- A flat bottom. A lot of roasting pans have a narrow channel around the inside edge of the pan. The raised center directs fat and drippings away from the food roasting in the middle of the pan. However, this also creates a troublesome situation when attempting to whisk ingredients into a smooth gravy. The channel creates a spot for food to get caught, and makes whisking more difficult.
- Sturdy construction. As mentioned above, roasting pans are often full of heavy food. A good roasting pan should be up to the task of supporting your 20-pound turkey without buckling or flexing under its weight.
Other Roasting Pans We Tested
- All-Clad Stainless Steel Flared Roasting Pan. This pan performed very well in testing and only missed out on the top spot due to its flat rack, which made transferring the pan in and out of the oven feel less secure. If, however, a flat rack is not a deal-breaker for you, this is a great option.
- Circulon Nonstick Roasting Pan. This pan’s thin construction led to overly dark chicken and unevenly cooked vegetables. The bottom of the pan has a ridged circular pattern and a channel around the inner rim, which makes whisking gravy difficult.
Frequently Asked Questions
- What’s the difference between a baking pan and a roasting pan? Baking pans are smaller than roasting pans and can be many different shapes and sizes. They’re used for everything from baking cakes to casseroles to brownies. Roasting pans are much larger than baking pans and usually include a rack to elevate the food from the bottom of the pan. They are designed to hold large pieces of meat and sometimes accompaniments like vegetables.
- Does a roasting pan need a rack? A rack elevates the food from the bottom of the pan, which helps with heat circulation and prevents burning. While we prefer an angled rack over a flat one, a rack of any style is key to cooking food well in a roasting pan.
- How do you clean a roasting pan? A roasting pan is quite large and not a great candidate for the dishwasher if you’d like it to stand the test of time. Hand-washing with soap and water is recommended to preserve the finish on roasting pans — steel and nonstick alike. For stainless steel models like our overall winner, a good scrub with a cleaner designed for steel, like Barkeeper’s Friend with a soft scrubbing sponge should do the trick. For nonstick models, soap and water and a soft scrubbing sponge should be enough to get them clean.

US government grounds all flights across the United States ‘due to extraordinary circumstances’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
21:44:38 UTC
06:44:38 KST

The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday afternoon that it has grounded all flights across the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances” and issues related to safety.
The FAA’s website said the cause is an “equipment outage.” The site itself was down for a brief period at the time of publication, with a note that the website was “experiencing technical difficulties.”
Per an alert sent by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC, the FAA said the ground stop means that aircraft cannot take off from departure gates. The message said that the disruption was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” but did not specify further. The alert was not visible on the ATCSCC website at press time.
The alert stated that all departing flights must remain on the ground “until further notice.” Inbound international flights will be “managed on a case-by-case basis,” it said.
A spokesperson for the FAA told TechCrunch that it issued the ground stop “following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” which manage the airspace across the United States.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a post on X: “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”
It’s not clear what caused the ongoing FAA equipment outage. The outage comes in the same week that the administration rolled out an AI-powered tool for air traffic controllers to save aircraft flight time and fuel costs — though it’s unclear if the ongoing outage is related.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that there is “no indication yet that this was a nefarious act,” but warned that the recovery “is going to take some time.”
Updated with comment from the FAA, and remarks from Homeland Security.

FAA ground stop shuts down flights nationwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
21:39:37 UTC
06:39:37 KST

Takeoffs from airports throughout the US largely stopped on Friday after the FAA issued a national ground stop at 3:44PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
FAA lifts nationwide ground stop that blocked takeoffs for hours
A communications problem shut down takeoffs across the US on Friday afternoon before it was lifted more than four hours later.
More than four hours after the stop was issued, officials announced it was lifted at 8:15PM ET and that flights will resume. It’s unclear how many flights will be able to take off and when, as they now face problems of overloaded airports and flight crews that have run out of time to operate the planes, meaning many people will be stuck where they are for the time being and more flights will be delayed or canceled.
In a White House press conference announcing that the stop had been lifted, Transportation Secretary Ryan Duffy blamed an aging air traffic control system that he is pursuing funds to replace, saying that the TRACONs (Terminal Radar Approach Control) in the air traffic control centers “started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and the communications from airplanes.”
He said that the devices that had the issue were analog telecom devices, where the switches / routers “got overloaded with data” and started to show inconsistency.
An earlier report from CBS News cited multiple sources who said that an update to the air traffic control system’s private communications network, operated by L3Harris, caused a system reboot and the subsequent outage. L3Harris has not yet responded to a request for comment from The Verge, but during the press conference, Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed that “patches” to the existing system sparked the issue.
In response to a reporter’s question about the patches and how they contributed to the outage, Duffy said, “By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system… I didn’t anticipate that we would have an outage like this.”
The flight tracking site FlightAware lists 9,124 US flights as delayed and 5,901 flights canceled as of 8:39PM ET.
According to CNN, the last nationwide ground stop in 2023 lasted for about 90 minutes after the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system for pilots went down, and the last one prior to that was after the attacks on September 11th, 2001.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Friday afternoon, Mullin told reporters that there is currently no reason to suspect a cyberattack or other national security threat, or any connection to the recent Microsoft Outlook outage, but that at the time no cause had been ruled out for the “telecommunications outage.”
When asked about any possible connection to the cloud-based AI Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system that was activated nationwide on November 10th, he said they were looking into that. Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company that designed the system and was awarded a 12-year $875 million contract in June to deploy it, denied any connection, tweeting “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”
Jon Ostrower of The Air Current reports that the outage began with the Chicago air traffic control center, followed by centers in Boston, Washington, New York, and Minneapolis, and as the FAA issued a ground stop for aircraft flying east, more facilities began reporting problems. He said the problems disrupted both the radar and radio frequencies used by air traffic controllers and pilots.
Updated, Friday, November 13th: Added that the stop has been lifted, and quotes from the press conference.

Mozilla to Shut Down Solo, Deleting Users' Websites and Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Mozilla to Shut Down Solo, Deleting Users' Websites and Data (theregister.com) 13
			
		 	
				Mozilla is shutting down Solo, its AI-powered website builder and hosting service, on November 30. A notice on the Soloist.ai homepage reads: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." The Register reports:  Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. Some 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them -- complete with custom domain names. Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code.

ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s Dots agents make purchases for you
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
20:45:10 UTC
05:45:10 KST

After launching its Dots AI agents platform earlier this year, OpenAI is launching a wallet for the agents. ChatGPT Wallet is rolling out starting today for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US aged 18 and older using a US billing address and “eligible US-issued American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa cards.”
ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s Dots agents make purchases for you
OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet won’t share your actual credit card info with its AI agents.
After adding a card to the wallet, your Dots agents can use it to buy things in response to your prompts, but they’ll check in with you each time before checking out. OpenAI’s support page says every purchase with ChatGPT Wallet requires a security check with biometric verification like Face ID or a fingerprint scan.
After you review the AI agent’s purchase and sign off on it, OpenAI says that, similar to using tap to pay, Apple Pay, or Google Wallet, it substitutes your credit card details with a payment token, so your actual card info isn’t shared with your Dots agent or the business you’re buying from. Eventually, OpenAI says it expects “users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases.”
ChatGPT Wallet might not work everywhere. Some retailers have restrictions on AI agents or block them altogether. Earlier this year, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agents. OpenAI says that in order for agents to use ChatGPT Wallet, “websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.”

Big tech is here to let us down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
20:20:30 UTC
05:20:30 KST

When I woke up this morning I thought about writing about the ongoing drama surrounding Nvidia and its morally and ethically corrupt leader. But, then I quickly saw the news about Microsoft Outlook going down, and with it Teams and Copilot.
I soon saw many employees celebrating what effectively became a "snow day for adults" as they literally couldn't do their jobs. Then I started seeing various businesses, ranging from small to medium, saying that their normal support services are unsurprisingly not working and instead to contact them via social media. Except, it's not just businesses that are impacted by Microsoft's incompetence. Even if this is some legitimate accident (and not a more likely instance of someone vibecoding their way via Copilot), when a company like Microsoft fires tens of thousands of employees, including many engineers, then these problems are not only more likely, but also more difficult to quickly fix. The fact that this has actually been an issue across two separate days is pathetic for a company like Microsoft.
As beyond businesses impacted, all sorts of other entities have been impacted. Various forms of educational institutions from schools to universities as well as the courts! I wouldn't be surprised if healthcare has been impacted as well.
Now, are Microsoft going to offer any compensation for either lost business or additional accrued costs? I highly doubt it, even though it is literally their fault and they do still have the cash reserves, despite increasingly wasting it on loss-making AI adventures.
This is a reminder of how indebted the Global North has become to Microsoft and its enshittified services. If most (but thankfully not all) businesses and institutions are deep into Microsoft systems, then when Microsoft inevitably messes up again, large swathes of organisations will not be able to function properly. Yes, it might be good for the individual worker in a generic office role, but for keyworker type organisations this can have really damaging implications. Many European state institutions have already started the move away from Microsoft to open source alternatives. Largely to not be at the mercy of an inconsistent United States of America, but also for times like this. As when Microsoft services go down, you cannot fix it! You have to wait for Microsoft to find a competent employee who wasn't let go to try and fix what was broken by some inept leftover who was deluded enough to think that Copilot can do everything.
I still want to talk about the issues of the impact of other US company Nvidia and the implications it has around the world. But that can wait for another day. Plus, who knows if another affairs comes out (we're currently at three).

This young startup wants to power floating data centers with the ocean’s heat, and investors are already on board
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
20:07:24 UTC
05:07:24 KST

Anyone who has weathered a hurricane can tell you that the oceans — which fuel the storms — contain a tremendous amount of energy. Thanks to global warming, they’re holding more than ever.
A new startup wants to harness that energy to power data centers.
Drogue, which has kept a low profile until now, is building a system that harvests heat from the ocean to power data centers on board floating vessels. According to founder and CEO Sam Sipe, the first prototype should be bobbing around the ocean, crunching bits, less than two years from now.
The goal, Sipe said, is to help data center developers deploy servers in AI-friendly timelines. “The data center industry is a real estate game, and so they’re playing on 8- to 10-year timelines, including interoperability with utilities and [independent system operators]” that manage regional power grids, he said. “AI demand has increased 10x in just the last three years. It’s completely incompatible.”
Drogue was founded just six months ago in Washington, D.C., and the startup told TechCrunch exclusively that it has already raised $20 million, including from XYZ Venture Capital, Toyota Ventures, Tamarack Global, Dream, FDVC, Garuda Ventures, Flexcap, Boost VC, and Slow Ventures, among other investors.
In those six months, Drogue has designed a multi-megawatt prototype that will be installed on a traditional oceangoing ship and sent out to sea in early 2028. Future versions will be built on floating structures that more closely resemble offshore oil platforms.
To Sipe, the decision to turn to the ocean was obvious.
After years flying E-2D Hawkeyes off U.S. Navy aircraft carriers, he had an appreciation for the ocean’s immense power. “Most people think, oh, ocean — hard waves, storms, corrosion, biofouling. And I just see this majestic place and resource that we just ignore,” he said.
As the planet warms, the oceans have been absorbing an additional 5.8 million terawatt-hours of energy every year. By comparison, all of human civilization uses about 180,000 terawatt-hours each year. If Drogue were to take some, surely the ocean wouldn’t miss it.
The startup’s technology works like a heat pump run in reverse. A heat pump uses electricity to move heat from one place to another; Drogue’s system instead uses a difference in temperature to generate electricity. This approach, known as ocean thermal energy conversion, or OTEC, was first developed in the 1950s.
Surface waters are warmer, heated by the sun, while down-deep temperatures are much colder, about 39°F on average (4°C). “There’s basically no amount of heat we can pull out of that that will collapse that temperature differential,” Sipe said.
To leverage the temperature differential, the startup’s system draws in warm surface water, uses it to cool the data centers, and then sends the now-warmer water to boil ammonia, a chemical that turns to gas at -28°F. That ammonia gas is then sent through a turbine to generate electricity. Once through the turbine, it courses through a condenser, which turns the gas back into a liquid. There, cold water drawn from 1,000 meters deep passes over the condenser’s fins to absorb the heat. The warmed water is then released, and dissipates into the ocean. The ammonia gets sent back to the start of the sealed loop, and the cycle repeats.
The basic idea was tested in the 1980s but tossed aside. “A lot has changed since the ’80s, specifically manufacturing techniques around the pipe and the heat exchangers,” Sipe said.
To find out why, Sipe sought out people who had worked on those early efforts. “I just talked to everyone, basically interviewed them and figured out what went wrong, what went right, what would you do next. And everyone was like, dude, this stuff works. It’s just a matter of being able to raise enough capital to build something big enough, because there’s a sweet spot,” he said.
There also had to be customers who could use that power while still at sea. Sending power to shore would require lengthy, expensive cables, and manufacturing on board would require similarly expensive shipping of materials and finished goods. Data centers are ideal — the servers are compact relative to other equipment, and shipping data off the platform is incredibly cheap. Each vessel would live at sea for about a decade, Sipe said.
Drogue already has “approval in principle,” a preliminary sign-off, from the American Bureau of Shipping, which sets and checks safety standards for ships. Now it’s in the process of buying its first ship to start building a prototype ready for the open ocean.
In many ways, Drogue’s concept is similar to Elon Musk’s plan for orbital data centers: find a cheap source of power, and get the data centers as close to it as possible. Except unlike orbital data centers, Drogue’s don’t need to launch expensive rockets to get there. They can just sail a ship on the ocean, something humanity has been doing for millennia.

Microsoft's Global Outage May Be Worse Than Amazon's Or Crowdstrike's, Expert Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

Microsoft's Global Outage May Be Worse Than Amazon's Or Crowdstrike's, Expert Says (arstechnica.com) 46
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: A global outage taking down a wide range of Microsoft 365 services remains ongoing Friday morning. The outage started midday Thursday, impacting users of Microsoft email, cloud, and AI services. Microsoft has documented the full list of services impacted by the error, while moving early Friday morning to protect customers around the world from losing emails during the extended disruptions. "Recovery actions are ongoing," the Microsoft 365 Status account confirmed on X. "To help preserve delayed mail during this event, we've extended email timeout to 48 hours."
Similar to recent world-shaking outages of widely used tech like Amazon Web Services and CrowdStrike, the Microsoft disruption looks like "one of the biggest outages of all time," Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, told NBC News. Possibly even "worse," he suggested.
Businesses, hospitals, police departments, and schools were among those scrambling to work around the outage. In Japan, it disrupted government IT infrastructure, according to deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki. NBC's report documented various harms, noting that "few public bodies were immune from the outage." In some cases, doctors couldn't send patients "important" updates on medication changes or follow-up care. The financial sector suffered, too, with people blocked from making bank transfers since they couldn't receive verification codes.
Justice systems were also hobbled. The Supreme Court in the Philippines saw its legal work derailed, NBC reported. And one US sheriff's office in Colorado reported that the outage made it difficult for people to post bond for prisoners' immediate release. It's unclear how many users were affected, but Microsoft estimated in January that the total number of paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions exceeded 450 million. Microsoft's most recent updates confirmed that it's seeing "broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific."
"Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation continues across remaining affected infrastructure," Microsoft said. "Our focus remains on stabilizing recovered infrastructure, completing mitigation in remaining impacted areas, and reducing delayed email queues and backlogs while we validate service consistency across connection methods."

I’ve Tested Multicookers for Decades — This Is the Best Instant Pot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
