I’ve Tested Multicookers for Decades — This Is the Best Instant Pot
Instant Pots have become a kitchen staple, making once-daunting tasks like pressure cooking inviting and offering myriad settings and uses in a single countertop appliance. These all-in-one appliances (or “multicookers”) offer an array of functions that can replace  the stovetop pressure cooker, slow cooker, and rice cooker that might be cluttering your cupboards. 
Higher-end models include specialized functions, such as yogurt making, sous vide, and even baking. Multicookers also excel at steaming fish, browning raw meat, cooking hot cereal, and hard-boiling eggs. You can even use one to help make Thanksgiving dinner!
Despite the many multicooker brands to choose from, Instant Pot remains one of the best-known. The wide range of Instant Pot models can be overwhelming, as the company rolls out ever more upgrades to beloved lines and updated versions with jazzy features. Whether you’re replacing an outdated model, downsizing (or upsizing) your current Instant Pot, or buying your first-ever multicooker, we have all the info you need.
Our Top Instant Pot Picks
Best Overall: Instant Pot Duo Plus 8QT Multi-Use Pressure Cooker ($159.99): With a full array of functions, easy-to-follow control panel, and well-designed pressure release system, the Duo Plus hits all of the high points at a mid-level price. It cooks small or large meals, and most components are dishwasher-safe.
Best Budget: Instant Pot Duo 6QT Multi-Use Pressure Cooker ($109.99): Instant Pot calls the Duo its “original all-in-one cooker,” and its functionality has stood up to the test of time. It remains a popular choice, holding fast against newer, often more expensive models.
Best for Small Kitchens: Instant Pot 4QT RIO Mini Multi-Cooker ($89.99): All the features in a smaller package make the Rio Mini ideal for tight spaces. It’s large enough to be useful and comes in standout colors.
Best Smart Cooker: Instant Pot Pro Plus 6QT Smart Multi-Cooker ($229.95): This Pro Plus smart model offers truly hands-off cooking, letting you control what’s happening inside the sealed cooker straight from your phone. Other advanced features and settings make this top-of-the-line multicooker worth the price tag.
Best Overall: Instant Pot Duo Plus 8QT Multi-Use Pressure Cooker
The Duo Plus line features several upgrades from Instant Pot’s classic model. The control panel contains a keep warm function, six standard cooking presets (pressure cook, slow cook, rice, steam, sauté, and yogurt), and adds sous vide and cake, which uses pressurized steam to bake cheesecake and more. A large, easy-to-turn control dial adjusts time, temperature, and settings. Other digital features include a cooking progress bar and a message bar with direct cooking instructions. Despite all of these options, the screen remains relatively easy to navigate.
Instant Pot has also quieted the steam release, upgrading it from the pressure release valve of older versions, and moved the vent to the opposite side of the release switch (read: farther from your fingers). The 8-quart size can make meals that serve six to eight people, and turn up to 1 1/2 gallons of milk into yogurt. A steaming rack and extra sealing ring extend its usefulness and lifetime. The removable stainless steel cooking pot, lid, and accessories can go straight in the dishwasher for effortless cleanup.
Best for: Everyone. The large-capacity, user-friendly Duo Plus can replace an array of appliances and tools in any kitchen, make meals large and small, and perform specialized tasks.

Best Budget: Instant Pot Duo 6QT Multi-Use Pressure Cooker
This 6-quart multicooker from the classic Duo line remains a workhorse in the kitchen at a lower price than upgrades with more bells and whistles. It handles loads of tasks, with seven cooking functions, including yogurt, and several pressure-cooking smart programs, like soup, meat or stew, beans, poultry, and porridge.
The control panel is all buttons and lights, with numerous options for adjustment. For example, if you’re pressure-cooking, you can shift the cooking time to match your recipe. You can also delay the start time so that a meal is ready when you walk in the door. The 6-quart size is ideal for feeding four to six people and is easier to store and less expensive than larger multicookers. Like many Instant Pot models, the lid and inner pot are dishwasher-safe.
Best for: Families that want to create meals easily and quickly without breaking the bank. Once you become familiar with the 6-quart Duo’s expansive features, it will become a reliable part of your cooking routine.

Best for Small Kitchens: Instant Pot 4QT RIO Mini Multi-Cooker
A multicooker can take up a lot of space in a tiny kitchen, but the 4-quart Rio Mini tucks right in. This Instant Pot is wide but shorter than larger models, making it easy to reach into and stir while sautéing. The squat little cooker is still large enough to be effective, pumping out three or four servings at a time, and has all of the essential functionality we’ve come to expect in multicookers.
Instant Pot has streamlined the control panel of this newer model, with labeled buttons for the six standard presets and icons for keep warm and other basic functions. The beginner-friendly design includes standard safety features, like an automatic lid lock — so that pressure has to be fully released before the lid can be opened — and automatic pressure and temperature control to keep both from skyrocketing. It also comes in multiple fun colors: choose from rosewater, truffle, salt, eucalyptus, or the classic black.
If you still have room for other appliances, Instant Pot has an entire Mini collection that extends to a standalone air fryer and a toaster oven with air fryer functions.
Best for: Small households and small kitchens. The 4-quart Rio Mini easily turns out single-serving meals, dinners for small families, and side dishes for bigger gatherings.

Best Smart Cooker: Instant Pot Pro Plus 6QT Smart Multi-Cooker
Instant Pot has wrapped many of its best features into this Pro Plus 6-quart multicooker. Then the company took it a step further by connecting the cooker to your phone, so you can monitor the process, make adjustments, and follow the app’s large collection of multicooker recipes.
The Pro Plus has two cooking functions found on few other models. NutriBoost simulates stirring inside the sealed unit when pressure cooking or steaming rice. This unit also brings back a canning function that was popular on some early multicookers; unfortunately, this has been shown to be unsafe by independent researchers and continues to be discouraged by food preservation experts, despite manufacturer claims.
Still, other upgrades make this smart model worth the price. From your phone, you can choose and save settings, track progress, and reset the timer while slow-cooking, or using the sous vide setting or pressure mode. The 3-ply stainless steel cooking pot has silicone handles so it’s easy to lift out while full for less messy serving.
Best for: Busy, tech-minded people who love smart appliances, and cooks who want pre-programmed recipes at their fingertips. Other high-end features sweeten the price of the 6-quart Pro Plus smart cooker.

Why You Should Trust Me
I have been a writer and editor for more than 25 years, with the last decade focused on food. I test and review kitchen products, write about cooking techniques and kitchen skills, develop recipes, teach cooking workshops, and work as a private chef. I also have decades of experience using pressure cookers and canning, and I’ve researched and tested various stovetop and digital cookers and canners.
What To Look For in an Instant Pot
- Size: Smaller Instant Pots are lighter, easier to store, and usually less expensive, but larger ones feed more people and often come with more functions and versatility. For nightly meals, choose a cooker with a quart capacity that matches the number of people you plan to feed.
- Power: Larger and newer models often have higher wattage, allowing them to pressurize faster and sauté and sear with more heat.
- Functions: Most Instant Pots perform the same basic functions, like pressure cooking, slow cooking, and steaming, but different models have different advanced functions, like sous vide and cake baking.
- Controls: Instant Pot control panels vary in design, and some are more intuitive and informative than others. Some may have a learning curve until they become familiar and comfortable.
- Adaptability: Options that let you adjust time, temperature, and pressure when using presets help when steaming delicate fish, crisping vegetables, and slowly braising a chuck roast.

Live-migration support in FreeBSD and bhyve coming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
19:58:42 UTC
04:58:42 KST

This project presents a first working state for live migration of bhyve guests on FreeBSD 15.1. A running amd64 guest can move between two hosts over TCP while continuing to run; it is paused only for the final stop-and-copy phase. The work builds on bhyve's experimental snapshot support and adds dirty-page tracking in the vmm kernel module together with a migration protocol in bhyve and bhyvectl.
I previously discussed the state of bhyve live migration, its historical development, existing limitations, and why it matters for the future of FreeBSD virtualization in my article bhyve on FreeBSD and VM Live Migration – Quo vadis?.
The goal is deliberately practical: make it possible to test, discuss, and improve a real implementation rather than discuss live migration only in the abstract. The current code and test tooling are being published as a WIP RFC so that the next steps can be shaped in the open. A more detailed demonstration of a VM being live migrated can be watched on my YouTube channel.
Why this matters
Live migration is an important building block for enterprise virtualisation. It enables host maintenance, hardware replacement, load balancing, and failure-domain management with far less disruption to workloads. It is also central to the Sylve project, which aims to offer a Proxmox-like virtualisation solution for FreeBSD. Migration is not an optional convenience in that kind of platform; it is one of the capabilities that makes clustered operations practical.
It is equally important for BoxyBSD, where I offer free BSD-based VPS instances to individuals. Without a credible migration path, routine host work can require a guest outage. That makes live migration a current show stopper for the project, and is why this work is being pushed toward a testable, reviewable state.
How the current implementation works
The source starts with a pre-copy phase. It sends populated guest memory, then repeatedly obtains a bitmap of pages changed since the previous scan and sends only those pages. Once the remaining dirty set fits the configured downtime target, stops shrinking, or reaches the configured round limit, bhyve pauses the guest and its devices. It then sends the final dirty pages and the existing snapshot state for the vCPUs, kernel state, and emulated devices.
The destination validates the basic VM geometry, receives memory and state, restores it, and reports that it is ready. Only then does the source send GO, the commit point. Before GO, a failed migration can resume the source guest. The destination does not start the guest if it does not receive that commit message. A warm, stop-and-copy mode is available too, which is useful both as a fallback and as a comparison baseline.
What is implemented today
- Pre-copy and warm migration: live pre-copy is configurable with downtime and maximum-round controls; explicit stop-and-copy migration is also supported.
- Multi-vCPU protocol support: the migration handshake carries the guest vCPU count, the destination refuses a count mismatch, and all guest vCPUs are paused and resumed as part of migration. The published test bed has primarily exercised a one-vCPU guest, so multi-vCPU stress and race testing remain required before making broader claims.
- Memory consistency checks: dirty-page tracking covers guest and mapped emulation writes through page dirty state, while vmm write holds are recorded separately. The test workload rewrites and verifies guest memory and reports any missing or stale page as a mismatch. Repeated ping-pong migrations have been used to check that the workload continues without errors.
- Disk-write validation: a guest-side workload repeatedly writes and fsyncs files, verifies checksums, and is checked again after a cold reboot. This is intended to exercise the device pause, drain, and restore path.
- Failure handling: destination refusal, an unreachable target, and a target disappearing during both pre-copy and stop-and-copy have been tested. Before commit, the source is intended to resume the paused guest after failure.
- Basic destination checks: protocol version, page size, memory layout, and vCPU count are checked before data transfer. The migration socket is opened by bhyvectl and passed into bhyve so that bhyve can remain inside its Capsicum sandbox.
- Supported scope: this is amd64-only and depends on the experimental BHYVE_SNAPSHOT support. It relies on snapshot-capable emulated devices; PCI passthrough is not migratablem, yet.
Observed results
In the current two-host test environment, repeated live migrations, memory-rewrite workloads, and fsync-heavy disk workloads have completed successfully. For a slowly dirtying 512 MiB guest, observed downtime has been roughly 138–171 ms. A rapidly dirtying guest may not converge during pre-copy, but still falls back to a correct stop-and-copy completion with a longer pause. These are encouraging engineering results, not a production support promise or a complete correctness proof.
Blockers before upstreaming can be evaluated further
The following are neutral engineering requirements, not criticism of the value of the prototype. They need to be addressed first before further upstreaming into FreeBSD can be evaluated responsibly.
- Prove and harden dirty-log correctness. The kernel-side dirty-page algorithm must be demonstrated not to lose a write while dirty bits are examined and cleared. It needs focused concurrency, paging, emulation-write, and multi-vCPU stress coverage, plus a reviewable locking and memory-ordering argument.
- Define a complete compatibility contract. Matching memory size and vCPU count is not enough. A destination should verify guest identity, CPU capabilities, bhyve/vmm and snapshot format compatibility, device topology and capabilities, and shared-storage identity before accepting a migration.
- Harden the transport and protocol. The current TCP transport has no authentication or encryption and uses a first-version native protocol. A stable protocol needs explicit wire formats, bounded message handling, timeouts, version negotiation, authentication or a supported external secure transport model, and clear operational guidance.
- Clarify the commit and device-side-effect boundary. The source/destination handoff must be reviewed so that device restoration cannot cause externally visible work before the source has committed, and so that the unavoidable uncertain outcome after a lost post-commit acknowledgement is operationally recoverable.
- Specify storage and network handoff. Shared storage must have defined coherency, durability, and fencing assumptions. Network migration also needs a clear answer for tap/bridge handling, MAC/IP movement, and traffic convergence.
- Build an in-tree test strategy. The current scripts and test-bed workloads are useful, but upstream review will need automated regression coverage and a documented support matrix across CPU counts, memory sizes, supported devices, host CPUs, and failure cases.
- Separate the work into reviewable patches. Dirty-page tracking, snapshot API refactoring, protocol/receiver work, CLI changes, and tests should be independently reviewable. This will make design feedback more actionable and reduce the risk of merging coupled changes.
Next steps
We have already had deeper discussions about these questions in the Sylve Discord. Publishing this current state is intended to make those discussions more concrete, bring in wider FreeBSD and bhyve feedback, and turn the prototype into a clear roadmap. The immediate focus is correctness, compatibility validation, transport safety, and repeatable tests—not adding performance features first. Currently, some peopel already have access to it and it's planned ot publish this at least as a proposal on my git and GitHub at:
- git.gyptazy.com/gyptazy/freebsd-bhyve-live-migration
- github.com/gyptazy/freebsd-bhyve-live-migration
Compression, zero-page elision, broader device coverage, richer orchestration, and performance tuning can follow once the foundation is sound. If you operate bhyve, work on FreeBSD virtualisation, or are interested in Sylve or BoxyBSD, testing the RFC and contributing design feedback would be especially valuable.
Status: WIP RFC for a first working bhyve live-migration implementation on FreeBSD 15.1.

Live-migration support in FreeBSD and bhyve coming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
19:58:42 UTC
04:58:42 KST

This project presents a first working state for live migration of bhyve guests on FreeBSD 15.1. A running amd64 guest can move between two hosts over TCP while continuing to run; it is paused only for the final stop-and-copy phase. The work builds on bhyve's experimental snapshot support and adds dirty-page tracking in the vmm kernel module together with a migration protocol in bhyve and bhyvectl.
I previously discussed the state of bhyve live migration, its historical development, existing limitations, and why it matters for the future of FreeBSD virtualization in my article bhyve on FreeBSD and VM Live Migration – Quo vadis?.
The goal is deliberately practical: make it possible to test, discuss, and improve a real implementation rather than discuss live migration only in the abstract. The current code and test tooling are being published as a WIP RFC so that the next steps can be shaped in the open. A more detailed demonstration of a VM being live migrated can be watched on my YouTube channel.
Why this matters
Live migration is an important building block for enterprise virtualisation. It enables host maintenance, hardware replacement, load balancing, and failure-domain management with far less disruption to workloads. It is also central to the Sylve project, which aims to offer a Proxmox-like virtualisation solution for FreeBSD. Migration is not an optional convenience in that kind of platform; it is one of the capabilities that makes clustered operations practical.
It is equally important for BoxyBSD, where I offer free BSD-based VPS instances to individuals. Without a credible migration path, routine host work can require a guest outage. That makes live migration a current show stopper for the project, and is why this work is being pushed toward a testable, reviewable state.
How the current implementation works
The source starts with a pre-copy phase. It sends populated guest memory, then repeatedly obtains a bitmap of pages changed since the previous scan and sends only those pages. Once the remaining dirty set fits the configured downtime target, stops shrinking, or reaches the configured round limit, bhyve pauses the guest and its devices. It then sends the final dirty pages and the existing snapshot state for the vCPUs, kernel state, and emulated devices.
The destination validates the basic VM geometry, receives memory and state, restores it, and reports that it is ready. Only then does the source send GO, the commit point. Before GO, a failed migration can resume the source guest. The destination does not start the guest if it does not receive that commit message. A warm, stop-and-copy mode is available too, which is useful both as a fallback and as a comparison baseline.
What is implemented today
- Pre-copy and warm migration: live pre-copy is configurable with downtime and maximum-round controls; explicit stop-and-copy migration is also supported.
- Multi-vCPU protocol support: the migration handshake carries the guest vCPU count, the destination refuses a count mismatch, and all guest vCPUs are paused and resumed as part of migration. The published test bed has primarily exercised a one-vCPU guest, so multi-vCPU stress and race testing remain required before making broader claims.
- Memory consistency checks: dirty-page tracking covers guest and mapped emulation writes through page dirty state, while vmm write holds are recorded separately. The test workload rewrites and verifies guest memory and reports any missing or stale page as a mismatch. Repeated ping-pong migrations have been used to check that the workload continues without errors.
- Disk-write validation: a guest-side workload repeatedly writes and fsyncs files, verifies checksums, and is checked again after a cold reboot. This is intended to exercise the device pause, drain, and restore path.
- Failure handling: destination refusal, an unreachable target, and a target disappearing during both pre-copy and stop-and-copy have been tested. Before commit, the source is intended to resume the paused guest after failure.
- Basic destination checks: protocol version, page size, memory layout, and vCPU count are checked before data transfer. The migration socket is opened by bhyvectl and passed into bhyve so that bhyve can remain inside its Capsicum sandbox.
- Supported scope: this is amd64-only and depends on the experimental BHYVE_SNAPSHOT support. It relies on snapshot-capable emulated devices; PCI passthrough is not migratablem, yet.
Observed results
In the current two-host test environment, repeated live migrations, memory-rewrite workloads, and fsync-heavy disk workloads have completed successfully. For a slowly dirtying 512 MiB guest, observed downtime has been roughly 138–171 ms. A rapidly dirtying guest may not converge during pre-copy, but still falls back to a correct stop-and-copy completion with a longer pause. These are encouraging engineering results, not a production support promise or a complete correctness proof.
Blockers before upstreaming can be evaluated further
The following are neutral engineering requirements, not criticism of the value of the prototype. They need to be addressed first before further upstreaming into FreeBSD can be evaluated responsibly.
- Prove and harden dirty-log correctness. The kernel-side dirty-page algorithm must be demonstrated not to lose a write while dirty bits are examined and cleared. It needs focused concurrency, paging, emulation-write, and multi-vCPU stress coverage, plus a reviewable locking and memory-ordering argument.
- Define a complete compatibility contract. Matching memory size and vCPU count is not enough. A destination should verify guest identity, CPU capabilities, bhyve/vmm and snapshot format compatibility, device topology and capabilities, and shared-storage identity before accepting a migration.
- Harden the transport and protocol. The current TCP transport has no authentication or encryption and uses a first-version native protocol. A stable protocol needs explicit wire formats, bounded message handling, timeouts, version negotiation, authentication or a supported external secure transport model, and clear operational guidance.
- Clarify the commit and device-side-effect boundary. The source/destination handoff must be reviewed so that device restoration cannot cause externally visible work before the source has committed, and so that the unavoidable uncertain outcome after a lost post-commit acknowledgement is operationally recoverable.
- Specify storage and network handoff. Shared storage must have defined coherency, durability, and fencing assumptions. Network migration also needs a clear answer for tap/bridge handling, MAC/IP movement, and traffic convergence.
- Build an in-tree test strategy. The current scripts and test-bed workloads are useful, but upstream review will need automated regression coverage and a documented support matrix across CPU counts, memory sizes, supported devices, host CPUs, and failure cases.
- Separate the work into reviewable patches. Dirty-page tracking, snapshot API refactoring, protocol/receiver work, CLI changes, and tests should be independently reviewable. This will make design feedback more actionable and reduce the risk of merging coupled changes.
Next steps
We have already had deeper discussions about these questions in the Sylve Discord. Publishing this current state is intended to make those discussions more concrete, bring in wider FreeBSD and bhyve feedback, and turn the prototype into a clear roadmap. The immediate focus is correctness, compatibility validation, transport safety, and repeatable tests—not adding performance features first. Currently, some peopel already have access to it and it's planned ot publish this at least as a proposal on my git and GitHub at:
- git.gyptazy.com/gyptazy/freebsd-bhyve-live-migration
- github.com/gyptazy/freebsd-bhyve-live-migration
Compression, zero-page elision, broader device coverage, richer orchestration, and performance tuning can follow once the foundation is sound. If you operate bhyve, work on FreeBSD virtualisation, or are interested in Sylve or BoxyBSD, testing the RFC and contributing design feedback would be especially valuable.
Status: WIP RFC for a first working bhyve live-migration implementation on FreeBSD 15.1.

No AI Slop: A Manifesto
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
19:51:56 UTC
04:51:56 KST

No AI Slop: A Manifesto
Written by the speakers and attendees of AIE Code Summit 2026
In 2001, 17 software engineers and leaders got together at a ski lodge in Snowbird, Utah to understand the biggest challenge of their time: heavyweight, documentation-driven software development processes.
Out of this we got the Agile Manifesto, four values and twelve principles that changed how most of the industry builds software.
Today we convene to build our own manifesto - the No AI Slop manifesto.
AI increasingly helps us write our code, docs, plans, and messages. We've all been on the receiving end of slop, and most of us have sent some too. Through this work, we have come to value:
Outcomes over output
Understanding over speed
Our own thinking over a model's first draft
Better work over easier work
Improving the system over patching the output
The world moves especially fast these days, but the goal of these resolutions is to embrace our important human role in harnessing AI safely, responsibly, in a way that creates value for everyone, and that will be relevant for years to come.
We believe:
- AI is the most useful tool most of us have ever worked with, but a swarm of agents can produce more work in a single day than a person can review in our lifetime.
- Slop is when we put less effort into producing something than we ask the consumer to spend understanding it.
- Using AI doesn't necessarily make something slop. Slop happens when we pass AI output along without taking responsibility for the quality or the reader's experience.
- AI cannot replace human judgement, it can only amplify our judgement (or lack thereof).
- Slop is asymmetric. The cost of producing a thousand-line PR or a ten-page doc is approaching zero, while the cost of reviewing it remains constant.
- In code, even before AI, slop proliferates when we repeatedly work around problems instead of solving them correctly. It comes from tools that lean HEAVILY toward adding rather than subtracting.
- A lot of slop comes from pressure. Companies are pushing their people to redefine what is humanly possible.
- Slop compounds. The more slop sits in our knowledge base, in chat, in code, the more of it the next agent reads and copies.
- The more slop flying around a team, the more we lose the will to fight it. Communication and quality get worse over time, not better.
Thus we the undersigned resolve that:
- Human time and attention is incredibly valuable, so we optimize for using it wisely.
- We fight slop because AI should make our work better, not just easier.
- We optimize systems, tools, and products for efficient elicitation of human intent and for efficient human understanding.
- We do our own thinking when working with a model. We explore resources, code, and prior art to truly understand the problem before the work starts.
- We own the intent, taste, and consequences of what we ship, however much AI helps us make it.
- When an agent wrote something we're sending, we make that clear, and we check the parts that matter before it goes out.
- When someone sends us slop, we tell them, kindly, and ask them to review it first. Most of us have needed that same note at some point.
- There will always be alpha in reviewing something. As models improve, we may stop reading most of the code. We may still review a plan, design, or result, because if we don't, we just get the same output as everyone else.
- Agent reviews, linters, and verifiers are useful but not sufficent. For now, we still review at least some subset of the outputs. What subset depends on the stakes.
- What shipped, who's using it, and how it's helping them matters FAR MORE than lines of code, prs merged, tokens spent, or the number of agents running in parallel.
- Unreviewed output isn't always necessarily bad. One-shot prompts and vibe coding are high leverage tools. "Slop" is bad when it undermines our outcome -- a useful product, a maintainable system, or saving ourselves and our teammates time and energy.
- When a mistake shows up twice, we scale ourselves and our team by improving the system and its guardrails. Anything a linter, type checker, or automated check can catch, we let it catch.
And finally:
- None of us has this figured out. We're each relearning what we will and won't accept, and there's no single right answer.
Again, the world moves especially fast these days, but the goal of these resolutions is to embrace our important human role in harnessing AI safely, responsibly, in a way that creates value for everyone, and that will be relevant for years to come.
We look forward to working with the community to evolve these beliefs as the world changes. Comments and feedback on this document are welcome. What is slop? Why does slop happen? Why is slop worth fighting? How do we fight slop?
Special thanks to Philip Kiely, Swyx, Lucas Meijer, Rebecca Bakels, Tejas Kumar, Natalie Serrino, Francisco Javier Arceo, Kent C. Dodds, Ankit Jain, Brandon Waselnuk, Mihail Eric, Justin McCarthy, Raz Berman Gold, Yacine Mahdid, Justin Poehnelt, Lauren Tan, and Kyle Mistele for contributions to this project.
More resources
- No More Slop - swyx declares war on slop, AIE Code Summit, November 2025
- Please stop the slop - Tejas Kumar on how he keeps slop out of his own writing
- Vibe Coding Our Way to Disaster - Jake Nations on why the thinking can't be handed to AI, only made bigger by it
- Ghostty AI Usage Policy - Ghostty Maintainers on the importance of human understanding and care
- Why Software Factories Fail - Dex begs us to please keep reading at least some of the code
Sign the manifesto
Sign the manifesto
Add a gist comment with any or all of: name, company, X handle, LinkedIn, and we'll regularly pull signatures into the manifesto.
Signed-off by: [any of: name, company, x, linkedin, etc]

Someone's Impersonating This Blog
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
19:41:09 UTC
04:41:09 KST

I was googling the name of my website, as one does occasionally, and was surprised to see a link to one of my blog posts on mataroa.site. At first I figured it was just an alternate domain name for mataroa.blog, but no, when you type mataroa.site into your browser, it shows you my blog. It's the only thing that's hosted there.
My next thought was that someone bought me a URL, but that can't be the case either: using a custom domain on mataroa requires a premium account, which I don't have. For anything but a plain redirect, I would have needed to set up the A record my end.
I then realized that the version of my blog on that site doesn't have the latest post. The most recent update on the homepage is my Aug 21 entry. When you scroll down and start clicking some of the older links, you get 404 pages. You also get a 404 if you try to post a comment, load the RSS feed or view standalone pages like the AI statement.
Someone scraped my blog and created a website to impersonate me. They're also impersonating mataroa, since using the name implies some sort of official connection.
They're re-hosting the stolen images on their own server, and they all have a watermark. Bizarrely, the watermark is mattbee.mataroa.blog, my real URL. I assume this is to somehow make it seem legitimate, like it's an officially-sanctioned mirror, but I don't know who they think is going to care. It's not like they're stealing from a site with name recognition.
When you view the source of a blog post, it's identical to the rendered HTML except that there are two Cloudflare scripts at the bottom, one to obfuscate the mailto: link in the footer (which doesn't work1) and one for analytics.
When you view the source of the index, there's a hidden link at the bottom to a Chinese github.io page for a website cloning tool.
I have no idea why I was targeted for impersonation. It should be obvious this isn't a high-value website.2 It's a personal blog where I write what's relevant to me, and that rarely overlaps with anything other people care about. If the subject matter didn't tip them off, it should be clear from the 0 comments on most posts that this is not an enterprise ripe for monetization.
If they just wanted a fake blog to scam adsense, surely a large language model would happily spew out more SEO-friendly slop than anything I have to offer. If their goal was to leech off the popularity of mataroa, why not impersonate one of the blogs with multiple front-page appearances on the orange website? Surely they have more SEO juice than me. Nothing about this makes any sense.
Anyway, the URL is registered with Namecheap, so I sent them an abuse report. I have no idea if they'll act on it. They don't seem to have a good track record of giving a shit unless the content is actually hosted with them.
It's hosted with Cloudflare, and the abuse reporting form they insist you use straight-up doesn't work. Click "Submit an abuse report" and it'll take you to a completely blank page. Very encouraging.
I'd have to dox myself to do a DMCA takedown, and I don't have the legal resources to do anything when it gets ignored. So if neither evil corporation cares to do anything, I guess I can just get fucked. I figure the best thing I can do to protect myself is document everything here. If you see a link to mataroa.site, it's not affiliated with me or mataroa. It seems like it isn't set up to scam people or distribute malware at the moment, but it probably will in the future. Be careful.
Edit
The index page also has a meta tag with a verification code for mitgo.com, a fake-looking website with some word salad identifying it as some kind of ad/SEO scamming platform or service. Will try to investigate this further.

AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation

Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.
That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.
LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.
With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.
True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well (case in point is newcomer Mintive). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

I Buy Bottle After Bottle of This Delicious Italian Olive Oil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
19:30:00 UTC
04:30:00 KST

I Buy Bottle After Bottle of This Delicious Italian Olive Oil
I have a love/hate relationship with gifting. I want to give everyone on my list a good gift. And by good I mean something that makes the receiver feel seen. In years past, that meant making a mental note when a friend chips a pie plate, or spending way too much time searching for a rustic set of picture frames for my brother-in-law’s office.
Unfortunately for me, loved ones aren’t regularly nicking their bakeware or starting new businesses, so sussing out these kinds of personalized gifts can be complicated. But fortunately for me (and them, and maybe even some of you), I found Piro, a premium bottle of olive oil that I can truly see anyone on this year’s list being thrilled to receive.
Piro Is One of the Best Olive Oils I’ve Ever Tasted
It’s not every day you watch freshly harvested olives — I’m talking picked from the trees in the morning and driven straight to the mill in the afternoon or overnight — become oil right in front of your eyes. But in November 2022, I traveled to Tuscany to witness first-hand the care and attention (and sleepless nights) the folks behind Piro put into making their award-winning oil.
Of course, it starts with high-quality ingredients. In this case, it’s olives, most of which are grown locally in Tuscany; the remaining arrive overnight in trucks from nearby Puglia. Once at the mill, the olives are cleaned before going through the crusher, which pulverizes them, followed by a malaxer (a trough with spiral mixing blades that stirs the olive paste for roughly 45 minutes until the oil starts to separate out).
The mix then goes through a series of centrifuges (first horizontal, then vertical) where the oil is separated from the pomace (pulp, crushed pits, water) and more particulate matter and water.
Now, here’s where Piro differs from other olive oils: Before bottling, the oil is filtered a third time. It passes through an air-pressurized dual lenticular filter — similar to the ones used in wine making — to remove even more particulate matter. (While chatting with co-founders Daniele Lepori, Romain Piro, and Marie-Charlotte Piro, I learned the machinery they use is a prototype and currently the only one of its kind being used in this way.)
This inventive process is, in part, how the olive oil received a gold award at the New York World Olive Oil Competition an impressive seven years in a row and a 97/100 from the Flos Olei in 2023, a prestigious international guide to extra-virgin olive oil. Beyond that, it’s what gives Piro a wonderfully robust flavor — the kind that lingers a bit and finishes with a peppery exclamation point. The high-antioxidant oil also has 25% of the daily value of vitamin E, although several other oils — sunflower, safflower, and soybean oil — are also rich in the nutrient. It is truly delicious enough to drink, which I did.
What’s the Best Way to Use Piro High-Antioxidant Extra-Virgin Olive Oil?
While slurping down olive oil is surely a good time (seriously, grab some friends, some bottles, a green apple to cleanse your palate, and have yourself a tasting party!), the hands-down best way to use this oil is often and with complete abandon. One night, I repeatedly drizzled it into an already delicious bowl of mushroom soup between bites. 10/10 recommend you try it.
It adds freshness and brightness to pizza, pastas, beet salads, and straight-up leafy greens. But don’t stop with those two: Sauté (or roast) your favorite vegetables with Piro and some seasonings. Same goes for your go-to meat and seafood dishes.
It’s surprisingly at home over pistachio cannolis, and I recommend you try drizzling some over your favorite pastries (hello, biscuits and croissants) and baked goods (cheesecake, anyone?). Or end the night a few scoops of just-as-luxe vanilla ice cream, a drizzle of olive oil, and some sea salt flakes for garnish instead of sprinkles.

Technology as a Search Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-13
19:27:15 UTC
04:27:15 KST

One of my ongoing research interests is understanding the nature of technological progress: How does new technology come into the world and improve over time? What sort of factors affect it? How, in general, should we think about it? I’ve come at this question from a few different angles: posts looking at the operations and legacy of Bell Labs, posts looking at how specific technologies improved over time, posts looking at how frequent multiple invention is and how long we wait for new inventions, and so on.
My current line of thinking is that creating some new technology is best thought of as a search process. A given technology can be thought of as a point in some high-dimensional “design space” or “technology space,” which contains every possible technology: every conceivable arrangement of parts, materials, natural phenomena, and so on. The job of the would-be inventor is to navigate this space, sifting through the arrangements of elements that don’t work to find the ones that will.
This search process is made difficult by the fact that, as with any situation where you’re enumerating the possible combinations of a large number of elements, technology space is incomprehensibly vast. In “Are Technologies Inevitable?” economist Matt Clancy notes that Wikipedia listed 272 “named equations” that describe various regularities in the world, ranging from the Navier-Stokes equations (which describe the motion of fluids) to the Arrhenius equation (which describes chemical reaction rates as a function of temperature) to the Exner equation (which describes how sediment gets deposited in a river). If we use this as a (very rough) estimate as to the number of different phenomena that a technology can leverage, it implies an enormous number of possible technologies that could be created. As Clancy writes:
If we’ve got 272 regularities to work with, for example, then the number of possible combinations of these regularities is two, raised to the power of 272 (since every regularity can be used or not used: two options). But 2^272 is more than some estimates of the number of atoms in the observable universe. And that’s got to be an undercount of the number of possible technologies, since it counts all technologies that use the same principles together as the same thing, even if they orchestrate them in vastly different ways or use them in vastly different magnitudes.
By comparison, the most common estimate for the number of atoms in the universe is around 10^80, or ~2^265. And it’s likely there are many, many more regularities that some technology could harness than 272. (Some in-progress work on this that I haven’t yet completed suggests that there are at least thousands.)
And as Clancy notes, this outrageously huge number dramatically undercounts the number of possible technologies, because it doesn’t take into account that the same phenomena can be used in lots of different ways. In Brian Arthur and Wolfgang Polak’s paper “The Evolution of Technology within a Simple Computer Model” (which we looked at earlier this year), Arthur and Polak note that even within the universe of logic circuits made up of three basic elements (the NAND gate and the values of 1 and 0), the number of different circuits you can make for even a small number of inputs and outputs is staggeringly large:
The emergence of circuits such as 8-bit adders seems not difficult. But consider the combinatorics. If a component has n inputs and m outputs there are (2^m)^(2^n) possible phenotypes, each of which could be realized in a practical way by a large number of different circuits. For example, an 8-bit adder is one of over 10^177,554 phenotypes with 16 inputs and 9 outputs.
So the search space for some new technology is vast. And the way that we tackle vast search spaces is with information. Each bit of information cuts a search space in half, so even a relatively small amount of information can quickly narrow down what seems like a huge search space. When we create some new technology, what we’re doing is gathering information: figuring out what will work and what won’t work, what’s promising and what isn’t, narrowing down the huge space of technological possibilities and finding something within it that accomplishes some particular goal.
In the 19th century, for instance, many people were interested in building a mechanical flying machine, but it wasn’t clear the exact arrangement of elements that would yield a successful one. Thanks to knowledge of the laws of physics, and an existence proof of birds, would-be inventors were already working within a considerably narrowed search space: they knew roughly what elements a flying machine would need to have — lifting surfaces, a propulsion system, and a means of control — and had a general idea of how they should be arranged. But there were a huge number of ways that you could build a flying machine from these basic elements, and people spent a great deal of time and effort building different sorts of machines that did not in fact work. The Wright brothers’ eventual success can in large part be attributed to the fact that they were exceptionally talented at gathering information, enabling them to converge on a working airplane design far faster than their competitors.
I previously explored the nature of technological search in that previous piece looking at Arthur and Polak technological evolution paper, which uses a simple simulation to evolve different logic circuits, finding workable technologies amidst an enormous sea of possibilities. I really liked the basic simulation method Arthur used in this paper — randomly generating technologies to see how easy or hard it was to find working ones — and wanted to use simulation myself to further explore the dynamics of technological search. But while Arthur uses digital circuits — different arrangements of logic gates like NAND, OR, AND, etc. that can perform functions like addition — I wanted a more general model that could capture the nature of many different types of technology, while still being simple enough to simulate easily.
The PTOP model
The model I came up with is inspired by another of Brian Arthur’s examinations of the nature of technology: his book The Nature of Technology. In this book Arthur describes technology as fundamentally “a set of phenomena captured and put to use.” He writes that:
… a practical technology consists of many phenomena working together. A radio receiver is not just a collection of parts. Nor is it merely a miniature signal processing factory. It is the orchestration of a collection of phenomena — induction, electron attraction and repulsion, electron emission, voltage drop across resistance, frequency resonance — all convened and set up to work in concert for a specific purpose.
Edison’s lightbulb, for instance, took advantage of several different phenomena: Joule heating, the phenomenon that electric current running through a material will raise its temperature. Incandescence, the phenomenon that a hot enough object will emit light. Transparency, the phenomenon that certain materials will allow the passage of light. And so on.
Phenomena like this are typically triggered automatically when the right conditions are created, which you can think about as being when the right objects, with the right properties, are placed in some particular arrangement. In the lightbulb, Joule heating occurs automatically when electric current runs through the filament, and incandescence occurs automatically when the filament gets hot enough. And the bulb had a vacuum atmosphere to prevent another, unwanted phenomenon — carbon reacting with oxygen — automatically occurring and destroying the carbon filament.
These three elements — Phenomena, Objects, and Properties — are the basic components of the technological model I came up with, which I call PTOP, for Phenomena Triggered by Objects with Properties. In this model you have some collection of objects, which can have some specified set of properties. Whenever the right objects with the right properties are placed in the proper arrangement, a phenomenon will be automatically triggered, which can have various effects: modifying the properties of existing objects, creating new objects, and so on. By chaining the correct objects and phenomena together in the correct order, you can create your desired outcome, which is some particular object or objects with some specific set of desirable properties. A simple, conceptual PTOP model for the lightbulb, for instance, might look like this:
By arranging the right sort of filament, an atmosphere, a bulb container, and electric current, you can trigger a series of phenomena that will ultimately result in the creation of light with desirable properties.
And here’s a sketch of a PTOP model for a more complicated technology, a Xerox machine, which uses various phenomena such as “photoconductivity” and “corona discharge” to generate a copy of a document:
I like this model because it captures the basic elements — natural phenomena and the conditions that trigger them — inherent to all types of technology, such that we can study the ‘space’ of possible technologies. And you can implement the basic idea in many different ways, from very simple representations of technology to very complex ones. In some ways this is bad (it took me a super long time, for instance, to come up with a simulable implementation that I was happy with) but it’s useful for studying different aspects of technological search. Let’s look at a few different implementations of a PTOP model and see what we find.
A level 1 PTOP model
Let’s start with an extremely simple version of PTOP. In this version, we have 10 possible objects, each with two possible properties. The first property, P0, can take on any value from 1 to 10 and is inherent and unique to that object. You can think of this as the model having 10 different chemical elements, each taking on a different value of P0. The second property is size, which can also take on any value from 1 to 10, but is adjustable. So you can have a large object with P0 equal to 1 and size equal to 10, or a small object with P0 equal to 1 and size equal to 1. Overall there are 100 possible sorts of objects: 10 different object types, each of which can be 10 different sizes.
This version of the model has four phenomena in total. Each phenomenon is triggered when the right two objects are connected, and the first of those objects (what we’ll call the input object) has the correct size. When the phenomenon is triggered, it adds a specific property to the second object (what we’ll call the output object). So in the image below, when an object with a P0 value of 1 and size 5 is connected to an object with a P0 value of 2, it triggers a phenomenon, which adds a new property, P1, to the second object.
The phenomena in this model are arranged in a hierarchy: triggering each phenomenon requires an object with the property added by the previous phenomenon. So to trigger the phenomenon that adds P2, you need an object with the P1 property. P3, in turn, requires an object with P2, and so on. You can think of this hierarchy of phenomena as representing something like “to trigger incandescence, I need an object with a high temperature. To achieve high temperature, I need to use the phenomenon of Joule heating, which I can trigger with the right sort of electric current. To create electric current, I need …” and so on.
In this version of the model, the goal is to create an object with the “final” property of P4. You can think of this as representing something like “light with the proper brightness” or “lead shot with the proper size and sphericity.” This can be done by creating the exact right arrangement of objects: five objects arranged in a line, each with the correct P0 property and size.
This is a very simple implementation of PTOP, which we’ll call a “level 1 model.” But it does capture a few things about the technological search process. First, the search space in even this very simple model is very large: 10 object types, 10 sizes, and 5 objects total means (10x10)^5 = 10 billion possible arrangements to produce a P5-level phenomenon.1 If you increased that to 100 objects, 100 sizes, and 10 different phenomena, you’d have 10^40 possible options. If we added more property types (maybe objects can have the properties of “temperature” and “density” in addition to size) the numbers would quickly become beyond astronomical.
But this simple version also shows the power that information can bring to bear on a large search space. When we looked at Arthur’s circuit search, we noted that what made the search tractable was modularity — finding a working design for a subcomponent, then locking that modular design into the system and using it as a repeatable ‘primitive’ element for further combinations. By preventing you from having to get every single part of a design correct in one shot, modularity effectively screens off many possibilities and reduces the size of the search space that must be traversed. As we found in that simulation:
A useful way of thinking about our 68 NAND gate search is that it’s like a huge, branching tree. At every step — every time we add a gate — there are thousands of branches, each one representing one possible way to wire up the gate. Each branch then splits into thousands more (representing all the possible ways of wiring up the next gate), which split into thousands more, which split into thousands more, until at the end we have 2^852 possible “leaves,” each one representing a unique way of wiring up all 68 gates. Trying to get all 68 gates right at once, and then checking to see whether or not you did, is like examining one single leaf, one path from the base of the tree all the way to the tip of a branch. Not only are you overwhelmingly likely to guess wrong, but you haven’t narrowed down your possibilities at all: all you know is that one single leaf wasn’t the right answer, leaving you with the rest of the 2^852 possible leaves to sift through.
Checking to see whether each gate we add is correct before we proceed to the next one, by contrast, massively narrows down the number of possibilities. Whenever we determine a gate isn’t in the right spot, it eliminates every possibility that branches off from that point. If there are 1000 possible ways to wire each gate, each time we guess correctly we’ve narrowed down the possibilities downstream of that choicepoint by 99.9%. Huge swaths of possibilities get eliminated at each correct guess, letting us converge on the correct answer much more quickly.
We can see these same basic mechanics with the PTOP model. With 10 object types, 10 sizes, 4 phenomena, and 1 billion effective possibilities, it takes (on average) 1 billion attempts to guess the entire correct design in one shot by randomly generating possible technologies.
But if we do a modular search — randomly adding just one object while randomly adjusting the size of the previous object until we’ve triggered the next phenomenon, then locking that successful design in and moving on — the search becomes much faster, because we’ve replaced a single billion-possibility space with a series of 100-possibility spaces. It takes on average 1,300 attempts to find the 10 type, 10 size, 4 phenomena answer, and even astronomically enormous technology space search problems become tractable.
This version also shows that the degree of modularity makes a huge difference in how easy a technology is to find. The more modules we have whose design we can lock in, the shorter each step is up the ladder to the working technology, and the easier each step is to take. If we take our 10 object type, 10 size model up to 100 phenomena levels, we’re now at an enormous 10^200 search space, but with 100 steps up the ladder that we can lock in, finding it is trivial — a random search finds it after about 10,000 attempts on average. The same-sized search space generated from 10 phenomena levels but 10 billion possible object types and sizes (which only gives us 10 steps up the ladder, rather than 100) becomes utterly impossible to find randomly, even with modular search.
This version of the model also lets us see how different sorts of knowledge can make the search process easier. For instance, as Joel Mokyr notes in The Gifts of Athena, scientific knowledge is very useful when trying to create some new technology, because “the range of experimentation possibilities that needs to be searched over is far larger if the searcher knows nothing about the natural principles at work.” In our level 1 PTOP model, scientific knowledge would be something like “phenomenon 3 can’t work with object type 2” or “phenomenon 4 must have its two objects of equal size.”
The usefulness of this sort of scientific knowledge is a function of how many possibilities it screens off. The more possibilities it screens off, the more bits of information it provides, and the more useful it is. So something like “phenomenon 5 can’t use object 1” or “object 3 can’t touch object 4” provides a relatively small amount of information, because it doesn’t eliminate that many possibilities. Knowledge of the sort “phenomenon 4 MUST use object 1” or “object 3 MUST touch object 4,” by contrast, screens off a lot more possibilities, provides much more information, and narrows the search much more effectively.
One reason that, in the real world, the technological development process is tractable is that a lot of our knowledge is of the latter type. Phenomena typically have specific triggering conditions, which we can observe and discover: Marconi knew what was needed to create electromagnetic waves when he was working on his radio, Edison knew what was needed to create incandescence in a lamp filament, and the scientists on the Manhattan Project knew roughly what conditions were needed to trigger a nuclear chain reaction.
A level 2 PTOP model
Even this highly simplified version of the PTOP model is useful for exploring various technological search dynamics. But ultimately it’s a little too simple to capture many of the more interesting dynamics of technological search. So let’s add some complexity. First, real phenomena often require multiple “input” objects, rather than just one: triggering the phenomenon of “combustion” in a gasoline engine requires fuel, an oxidizer, and an electric spark. So we’ll make it so that each phenomenon can have multiple input objects instead of just one. Second, there are often multiple different phenomena that you can use to accomplish some particular goal: if you want to make mechanical motion, for instance, there are a variety of different phenomena you can harness to do that, and motors built to harness them — electric motors, hydraulic motors, internal combustion engines — all work in different ways. So let’s also make it so that instead of just one phenomenon for each level, there can be more than one, each one requiring a different set of objects with the right properties to trigger.
With the level 1 PTOP model, there was only a single workable version of the technology. With the level 2 model, there are multiple working designs. And unlike the straight lines of objects of the previous model, this one creates branching, treelike chains.
With this version of the model (which I’ll call the “level 2 model”), even though there are a large number of possible working designs, the number of nonworking technologies is vastly larger, and finding a workable option by pure blind search quickly becomes unworkable.
We can solve this with a slightly different flavor of modular search, very similar to the “encapsulation” that Arthur uses in his technological evolution paper. In this version, the model starts out by randomly combining different objects with different properties, connected in different ways. Whenever an arrangement of objects triggers some phenomena, that arrangement gets bundled into a new object, and then that object can be chosen by the simulation to be randomly combined with other objects. As with our previous, simpler modular search, this lets the simulation accumulate partial solutions and quickly find working technologies even amidst very large search spaces.
A level 2 PTOP model can also be used to show the information-accumulating power of sexual reproduction. In a previous essay, we noted that sexual reproduction is its own sort of modular search — by letting children inherit genes from two parents, sex allows useful genetic “discoveries” made by many different lineages to spread throughout the population. This is in contrast to asexual reproduction, where only one particular lineage ultimately survives, and discoveries made by others die out due to a phenomenon called “clonal interference.” This allows sexually reproducing populations to converge on maximum fitness much more quickly.
We can see this same thing using the level 2 PTOP model. I ran a version of it with two different technology “populations.” Each population had 1,000 randomly generated technologies in it. In one population, I implemented asexual reproduction — each generation, every technology would get one random mutation to an object (deleting an object, adding an object, or changing an objects properties). The fittest members of the population, measured by the highest phenomena level they had unlocked, survived into the next generation. In the other population, I implemented sexual reproduction — in addition to random mutation, children would be generated by randomly crossing over the branches of two parents. With 5 levels of phenomena, asexual reproduction couldn’t achieve the maximum phenomena level after 2,000 generations in the example below; sexual reproduction, by contrast, found it after just over 100 generations.
A level 3 PTOP model
This flavor of PTOP is a little richer and can show a broader array of technological search dynamics, but it’s still a little simple, so let’s add some more complexity.
First, instead of making triggered properties — P1, P2, P3, etc. — binary (on or off), let’s make them be able to take on multiple values: before the property is switched on, it has a value of 0, while once a phenomenon triggers it, it can have a value from 1 to 10. We’ll make the value that it takes a function of two things: the size of the input object(s) and the value of the predecessor phenomenon. So for a phenomenon that triggers P2, the value of P2 will depend on the value of P1 and the size of its object. You can think of this as representing something like “the temperature in the lightbulb filament depends on the properties of the electric current flowing through it”: more amperage, or higher voltage, means higher filament temperatures. The brightness of the light emitted, in turn, will be a function of the temperature value of the filament.
We’ll make the value of triggered phenomena be determined in one of two ways. Either it’s maximized when the predecessor phenomenon and object size are EQUAL, or maximized when they’re as different as possible. So P2 can either be 10 when P1 and its size are the same (both 1, both 2, both 3), or when one is 10 and the other is 1. (For phenomena triggered by multiple input objects, we’ll take the average of the value calculated for each object.) We’ll call this version of the PTOP model the “level 3 model.”
This change actually makes the initial stage of the technological search much easier. Because the correct object size is no longer needed to trigger a phenomenon (just the correct object type), getting a technology that triggers the final phenomenon is now very easy (though it would be easy to change this by making the value of triggered phenomena dependent on some new property instead of size, and keeping whether or not a phenomenon is triggered size dependent). But now there’s an element of performance tuning. A technology that works, in the sense that it has a positive value for the final triggered phenomenon, might be quick to find, but to maximize performance — achieve a final phenomenon with a value of 10 — you need to keep iterating, fiddling with the sizes of the various objects to gradually push performance up.
This dialing-in step is meant to capture the technological development process: taking some technology that already works to some degree and pushing its performance higher or building a version that works in a particular way. With Edison’s lightbulb, for instance, incandescent bulbs had been demonstrated since the early 19th century, but their performance was poor — they burned out quickly, or the interior of the bulb blackened, or they used too much power. Edison took a technology whose configuration had been mostly figured out — a high-melting-point filament, a glass bulb, and an atmosphere to minimize reactivity were all common characteristics of previous bulbs — and pushed its performance higher by tweaking the properties of the various elements: the level of vacuum, the size of the filament, the exact type of carbon, and so on.
In the level 2 model, we had multiple phenomena for each level — multiple different ways to trigger P2, for instance. In the level 3 model, we’ll keep the same feature, but we’ll add a twist: different phenomena have different ranges for triggered properties that they can possibly achieve. So one way of triggering P2 might only be able to reach a value of 7, while the other might be able to achieve a value of 10. For some technologies, this might be fine; in other cases, maximizing performance will require using some other, different phenomena instead.
This also mirrors what we see with real-world technologies. When developing some new technology, the designer will be confronted with many possible ways of doing some particular job, and depending on the performance required, different options might work best. In the lightbulb, the performance of a carbon filament could only be pushed so high, and so eventually lightbulbs switched to tungsten filaments, which in turn required inventing a new process for producing ductile tungsten wire. Similarly, there are a variety of different ways of implementing the valves on an internal combustion engine to let gases into and out of the cylinders. Achieving very high engine performance, such as the number of revolutions per minute required on a Formula One car, requires complex valves that use things like compressed air instead of conventional wire springs, while if you’re building a four-door sedan the cheaper and simpler wire spring is fine.
Let’s now add one more element to the level 3 model. Up until now, we’ve had one single chain of properties: one phenomenon triggers another, which triggers another, and so on. Now let’s add a parallel set of properties, triggered by a parallel set of phenomena. In our lightbulb example, we can think of this as the temperature of the filament triggering not only incandescence but thermal expansion and thermionic emission.
(In this example, all these phenomena are triggered by the same property, temperature. In our model, for ease of modeling purposes we’ll have each of the parallel phenomena triggered by its own property.)
These parallel phenomena are triggered under the same conditions as the primary phenomena, but their values might not necessarily be determined in the same way: the conditions that create a value of 10 for P2 might create a value of 5, or 1, for parallel property T2. Ultimate performance of a technology will be a function of both of the final triggered properties: the value of, say, not just P9 but T9 as well.
This addition has a few consequences. For one, the technological search becomes more difficult: trying to dial in a technology by adjusting sizes randomly takes many more iterations if you’re trying to maximize both P9 and T9 than it does if you’re just trying to maximize one or the other. This mirrors technology more generally: the more dimensions of performance you care about, the more difficult getting a technology that’s good enough is.
Another consequence of this addition is that we now have design trade-offs. With multiple phenomena (and parallel phenomena) at each level, we can have different designs, which might achieve different levels of performance. I ran a level 3 search that generated random technological prototypes, and then tried to dial in the performance of each one for several different performance goals: maximizing P7 and T7, minimizing them, and achieving some specific value for each. At the end of the run, each goal had a fundamentally different arrangement, with different values for object sizes. The same basic technology was best implemented in different ways, depending on the performance goal.
Conclusion
To understand the nature of technological progress, it’s useful to think of creating a new technology as a sort of search process, one that’s made tractable by the intelligent acquisition and application of information. We can understand technological progress, in turn, by studying the nature of search processes — what sort of things make them easy, what sort of things make them hard, what sort of information acquisition methods we can bring to bear, and so on. The PTOP models described above are, I think, a useful tool for exploring these technological search dynamics: they’re simple to simulate, they’re flexible, and they can capture a lot of real-world elements of technological development.
The actual search space is 1 billion, not 10, because the size of the last object doesn’t affect any phenomena.
